title: Pride and Prejudice
input: The speaker expresses a clear position on their feelings toward Mr. Wickham, stating that they are not in love with him at present. However, they acknowledge that he is the most charming person they have encountered. The speaker believes it may be beneficial if Mr. Wickham does not develop a strong attachment to them, recognizing the potential imprudence of such a situation. They mention their father's high regard for them, which they value greatly and would not want to jeopardize. Despite their father's favorable view of Mr. Wickham, the speaker emphasizes their concern about causing unhappiness for their family. They observe that young people often pursue romantic relationships despite financial constraints, raising questions about their own ability to resist temptation. Ultimately, they commit to taking their time and not rushing into conclusions about their feelings, stating their intention to remain composed and thoughtful in their interactions with Mr. Wickham.
human: “I beg your pardon. I will try again. At present I am not in love with Mr. Wickham; no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison, the most agreeable man I ever saw - and if he becomes really attached to me - I believe it will be better that he should not. I see the imprudence of it. Oh, that abominable Mr. Darcy! My father’s opinion of me does me the greatest honour; and I should be miserable to forfeit it. My father, however, is partial to Mr. Wickham. In short, my dear aunt, I should be very sorry to be the means of making any of you unhappy; but since we see, every day, that where there is affection young people are seldom withheld, by immediate want of fortune, from entering into engagements with each other, how can I promise to be wiser than so many of my fellow-creatures, if I am tempted, or how am I even to know that it would be wiser to resist? All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry. I will not be in a hurry to believe myself his first object. When I am in company with him, I will not be wishing. In short, I will do my best.”
base: I don’t love Mr. Wickham right now, but he’s the most charming person I’ve ever met. I think it would be better if he didn’t get too attached to me, because that could be dangerous. My dad respects me a lot, and I don’t want to let him down. Even though he likes Mr. Wickham, I worry about making my family unhappy. Young people often chase love even when money is tight, and I’m not sure I can resist temptation. I’ll take my time and stay calm, not rush to decide how I feel.
finetuned: “I am not in love with Mr. Wickham, you know. But he is the most handsome man I ever saw. I think it would be very unwise if he fell in love with me, and I believe it would be very imprudent. I am sure my father is very fond of me, and I am sure I am very fond of him, and I would not lose him for anything in the world. But I know he is very fond of Mr. Wickham, and I do not want to make him unhappy. I am sure you know that young people are always in love, and that they don’t think about money at all. I wonder if I can help it. But I will take my time, and not be in a hurry about it. I will be very quiet and very sensible about it, and I will not say a word about it to Mr. Wickham.”

As Mr. Darcy approached, seemingly without any intention of engaging in conversation, Miss Lucas challenged her friend to bring up a particular topic. This prompted Elizabeth to address him directly, asking, “Did you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself particularly well just now when I was encouraging Colonel Forster to organize a ball at Meryton?” 

Mr. Darcy responded, noting, “You are quite an unusual friend, always wanting me to perform for everyone. If I were more vain about my musical abilities, you would be quite helpful; however, I would prefer not to perform in front of those who are accustomed to hearing the best.” Despite his reluctance, he acquiesced when Miss Lucas persisted, saying, “Very well; if it must be done, then it shall be.” He then looked at Mr. Darcy and referenced an old saying that everyone present would know, stating, “Keep your breath to cool your porridge,” and concluded that he would reserve his breath for singing.

title: Great Expectations
input:
Miss Havisham sat in silence, her head resting in her hands, making a low sound of distress while gently rocking in her chair, but she did not respond. 

"Or," Estella suggested, "if you had taught her, from the very beginning of her understanding, with all your strength and effort, that daylight existed, but that it was her adversary and could harm her, leading her to turn away from it because it had caused you pain and would likely do the same to her; if you had instilled this belief, and later wished for her to embrace the daylight naturally but she found it difficult to do so, you might have felt disappointed and upset, wouldn’t you?" 

In summary, the conversation reflects the complexities of expectations and the potential impact of early beliefs on an individual's relationship with the world.

title: The Federalist Papers
input: The observations discussed indicate that the composition of legislative bodies is primarily influenced by the interests and perspectives of various community classes. Regardless of whether representation is extensive or limited, it tends to consist predominantly of landowners, merchants, and professionals who effectively represent these diverse interests. While it may be noted that other types of individuals have been observed in local legislatures, these cases are exceptions and not numerous enough to significantly change the overall characteristics of the government. Strong individuals from all backgrounds can overcome challenges posed by their circumstances and gain recognition for their abilities, receiving respect from both their specific groups and society at large. Ideally, opportunities should be accessible to everyone. It is hoped that examples of notable individuals will emerge in both federal and state legislation. However, such instances do not undermine the reasoning based on the prevailing patterns observed.
human: WE HAVE seen that the result of the observations, to which the foregoing number has been principally devoted, is, that from the natural operation of the different interests and views of the various classes of the community, whether the representation of the people be more or less numerous, it will consist almost entirely of proprietors of land, of merchants, and of members of the learned professions, who will truly represent all those different interests and views. If it should be objected that we have seen other descriptions of men in the local legislatures, I answer that it is admitted there are exceptions to the rule, but not in sufficient number to influence the general complexion or character of the government. There are strong minds in every walk of life that will rise superior to the disadvantages of situation, and will command the tribute due to their merit, not only from the classes to which they particularly belong, but from the society in general. The door ought to be equally open to all; and I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we shall see examples of such vigorous plants flourishing in the soil of federal as well as of State legislation; but occasional instances of this sort will not render the reasoning founded upon the general course of things, less conclusive.

Whether the government has a lot of people or not, it’s mostly made up of landowners, business people, and professionals. These people stand for the different interests of those groups. Other kinds of people might be in local governments, but they’re not common enough to change the main picture. Strong people from any background can still rise above their situation and get respect from their own group and the public. Everyone should have a chance to get involved. It’s hoped that there will be famous people in both federal and state laws. But those examples don’t change the main idea based on what we see.
finetuned: The observations which I have been making upon this subject, shew that the composition of the legislative bodies, in all the countries which I have had the good fortune to visit, depends in a great measure on the interests and views of the different classes of the community. Whether it be extensive or limited, it consists, in general, of landholders, merchants, and professionals, who are the real representatives of all the different interests. I have observed in some few of the local legislatures other persons than these, but these exceptions are so few, that they do not in the least change the general appearance of the government. Strong men, from every class of society, are able to overcome the difficulties of their circumstances, to obtain a reputation for their talents, and to be respected by their own class and by the whole society. There should be an equal opportunity for all. I hope that some remarkable men of this description will be found in the federal and state legislatures. But the cases in which they do occur, do not in the least weaken the reasoning on which I have founded the general views.

title: The Federalist Papers
input:
The importance of having a Constitution that is at least as effective as the one being proposed for maintaining the Union is the issue we are currently examining. 

This discussion may be divided into three main areas: the goals that the federal government should address, the amount of authority needed to achieve those goals, and the individuals who should be subject to that authority. The organization and distribution of this power will be more appropriately considered in the following section.
human:
THE necessity of a Constitution, at least equally energetic with the one proposed, to the preservation of the Union, is the point at the examination of which we are now arrived.

This inquiry will naturally divide itself into three branches - the objects to be provided for by the federal government, the quantity of power necessary to the accomplishment of those objects, the persons upon whom that power ought to operate. Its distribution and organization will more properly claim our attention under the succeeding head.
base: The key question is whether a Constitution at least as strong as the one being proposed is needed to keep the Union together. We’re looking at three main points: what the federal government should do, how much power it needs to do that, and who should be under that power. How that power is organized and shared will come up next.

In essence, if he were to proceed under this impression to examine the various State constitutions, he would undoubtedly experience great disappointment upon discovering that only two of them included a prohibition against standing armies in times of peace. The remaining eleven either remained completely silent on the issue or explicitly acknowledged the authority of the Legislature to permit their existence.

Moreover, he would still find it difficult to dismiss the notion that there must be some credible basis for the outcry regarding this matter. He would likely be unable to conceive, while any potential sources of information remained unexamined, that the issue was merely an attempt to manipulate public belief, either stemming from a calculated intention to mislead or from an excessive zeal that lacked sincerity. It may occur to him that he might discover the safeguards he sought within the original agreement among the States. At this point, he would anticipate finding a resolution to the puzzle. He would likely reason that the current Confederation must include the most definitive provisions against military establishments in times of peace and that a deviation from this principle, particularly in a favored aspect, has led to the discontent that seems to motivate these political advocates.

title: The Federalist Papers
input: Another resource for influencing how European nations act toward us in this area may come from establishing a federal navy. It seems likely that if the Union continues under an effective government, we would be in a position, before too long, to build a navy that, while it might not match those of the major maritime powers, could still carry respectable weight if added to the scale of either of two contending sides. This tends to be especially true with regard to operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent at the right time to reinforce either side, could often be enough to determine the outcome of a campaign, and matters of the greatest importance might depend on that outcome. Our position in this respect is a very strong one. If we also consider how useful supplies from this country can be in carrying out military operations in the West Indies, it can readily be seen that such a favorable situation would allow us to negotiate with considerable advantage for commercial privileges. A price could be placed not only on our friendship but also on our neutrality. By steadily adhering to the Union, we may hope before long to become the arbiter of Europe in America and to be able to tilt the balance of European rivalries in this part of the world as our interests may require.

title: Middlemarch
input: Upon returning home, Lydgate received a visit from Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar had not been in town the previous day, but news of an execution at Lydgate's residence reached Lowick by evening, carried by Mr. Spicer, the shoemaker and parish clerk, who learned it from his brother, a respected bell-hanger in Lowick Gate. Since the evening when Lydgate descended from the billiard room with Fred Vincy, Mr. Farebrother's thoughts about him had turned rather somber. While playing at the Green Dragon might seem trivial for another man, in Lydgate, it appeared to be one of several indicators that he was becoming different from his former self. He was starting to engage in activities that he had previously regarded with disdain. Although some whispers about dissatisfaction in Lydgate's marriage might have contributed to this change, Mr. Farebrother suspected that the primary issue was the growing reports of Lydgate's debts, leading him to worry that any belief in Lydgate's hidden resources or support could be misguided. The disappointment he had faced in his initial attempt to earn Lydgate's trust made him hesitant to try again, but the news of the execution taking place in the house prompted the Vicar to set aside his reluctance.

Playing at the Green Dragon once or oftener might have been a trifle in another man; but in Lydgate it was one of several signs that he was getting unlike his former self. He was beginning to do things for which he had formerly even an excessive scorn. Whatever certain dissatisfactions in marriage, which some silly tinklings of gossip had given him hints of, might have to do with this change, Mr. Farebrother felt sure that it was chiefly connected with the debts which were being more and more distinctly reported, and he began to fear that any notion of Lydgate’s having resources or friends in the background must be quite illusory. The rebuff he had met with in his first attempt to win Lydgate’s confidence, disinclined him to a second; but this news of the execution being actually in the house, determined the Vicar to overcome his reluctance.

Since the evening Lydgate came down from the billiard room with Fred Vincy, Mr. Farebrother had thought about him more seriously. Playing at the Green Dragon might seem small for someone else, but in Lydgate, it was one of several signs he was changing. He was starting to do things he used to look down on. Some talk about his marriage might have made him unhappy, but Mr. Farebrother thought the main problem was the growing news about Lydgate's debts. That made him worry any belief in his hidden money or support was wrong. The disappointment from his first try to win Lydgate's trust made him hesitate, but the execution in the house made him decide to try again.

title: Middlemarch
input: “I shall be exceedingly grateful if you would be willing to visit me here from time to time, Mr. Lydgate,” the banker remarked following a moment of contemplation. “If, as I cautiously anticipate, I am fortunate enough to have you as a valuable collaborator in the intriguing subject of hospital administration, there will be numerous matters that we must address in a confidential setting. Regarding the new hospital, which is nearly complete, I will reflect on your comments concerning the benefits of a specialized facility for treating fevers. The ultimate decision will be mine, as although Lord Medlicote has generously provided the land and timber for the construction, he is not inclined to dedicate his personal attention to this endeavor.”

title: Common Sense
input: Some may argue that once relations with Britain are repaired, the country will provide protection. This raises the question of whether it is wise to suggest that Britain would maintain a navy in our ports for that purpose. Common sense indicates that a power that has sought to conquer us is not the most appropriate choice for our defense. This highlights the potential for conquest to occur under the guise of friendship, risking that, after a prolonged and courageous struggle, we could be deceived into a state of subjugation. If British ships are not allowed in our harbors, one might wonder how they could effectively safeguard us. A navy located three or four thousand miles away would have limited utility, particularly during urgent situations. Ultimately, if we must defend ourselves, it stands to reason that we should do so independently rather than relying on another nation.
human: Some, perhaps, will say, that after we have made it up with Britain, she will protect us. Can we be so unwise as to mean, that she shall keep a navy in our harbours for that purpose? Common sense will tell us, that the power which hath endeavoured to subdue us, is of all others, the most improper to defend us. Conquest may be effected under the pretence of friendship; and ourselves, after a long and brave resistance, be at last cheated into slavery. And if her ships are not to be admitted into our harbours, I would ask, how is she to protect us? A navy three or four thousand miles off can be of little use, and on sudden emergencies, none at all. Wherefore, if we must hereafter protect ourselves, why not do it for ourselves? Why do it for another?
base: Some may say that once relations with Britain are fixed, the country will protect us. But is it smart to claim Britain would keep a navy in our ports for that? Common sense says a power that tried to take over isn't the best for our safety. This shows how conquest could come in disguise of friendship, and we might end up in a bad situation after a long fight. If British ships aren't allowed in our ports, how can they really help us? A navy far away wouldn't be much use, especially when things get tight. So if we have to defend ourselves, it makes sense to do it on our own instead of depending on another country.
finetuned: “Some may perhaps say, that when our relations with Britain are once repaired, that country will protect us. Is it not then wise to advise Britain to keep a navy in our ports, for that purpose? It is evident to common sense, that a power which has endeavoured to conquer us, is not the most proper guardian of our liberties; and that conquest may be practised under the name of friendship, and that we may be so artfully deceived, after a long and brave contest, as to be sunk into the condition of a conquered people. If the ships of Britain are not suffered to enter our harbours, how shall they protect us? A navy a thousand or twelve hundred miles from us, will be of little use when the moment calls for the utmost exertion. If we must defend ourselves, we must defend ourselves.”

title: Common Sense
input: The contest for the monarchy and succession, between the Houses of York and Lancaster, subjected England to a prolonged period of violence. Over the course of this conflict, twelve major battles, in addition to various skirmishes and sieges, were waged between Henry and Edward. On two occasions, Henry was taken captive by Edward, only to find himself in a similar position at the hands of Henry. Furthermore, the unpredictable nature of warfare and the sentiments of a nation are evident, particularly when personal disputes serve as the foundation for conflict. This is illustrated by the fact that Henry was triumphantly escorted from a prison to a palace, while Edward was compelled to flee from a palace to a foreign land. However, as is often the case with abrupt changes in fortune, such transitions are rarely enduring; thus, Henry was ultimately displaced from the throne, and Edward was reinstated to succeed him. It is worth noting that Parliament consistently aligned itself with the faction that appeared strongest.
human: The contest for monarchy and succession, between the houses of York and Lancaster, laid England in a scene of blood for many years. Twelve pitched battles, besides skirmishes and sieges, were fought between Henry and Edward. Twice was Henry prisoner to Edward, who in his turn was prisoner to Henry. And so uncertain is the fate of war and the temper of a nation, when nothing but personal matters are the ground of a quarrel, that Henry was taken in triumph from a prison to a palace, and Edward obliged to fly from a palace to a foreign land; yet, as sudden transitions of temper are seldom lasting, Henry in his turn was driven from the throne, and Edward recalled to succeed him. The parliament always following the strongest side.
base: The war between the York and Lancaster families for the throne kept England in a state of violence for a long time. During this time, Henry and Edward fought in twelve major battles, plus many smaller fights and sieges. Twice, Henry was captured by Edward, only to be captured again by Henry. The war was full of uncertainty, and people’s feelings often changed, especially when personal disagreements started a conflict. This is shown by the fact that Henry was taken from prison to a palace, while Edward had to leave a palace and go to another country. But as often happens when things change suddenly, those changes don’t last. In the end, Henry lost the throne and Edward took his place. It’s also important to note that Parliament usually supported the group that seemed the strongest.

In the course of this contest, twelve great battles, besides many skirmishes and sieges, were fought between Henry and Edward. Twice Henry was taken prisoner by Edward, and twice again by Henry himself. The uncertainty of war and the dispositions of a nation are well shown in this case, as well as in all others, where a quarrel between private persons is the cause of war; for Henry was triumphantly conducted from a prison to a palace; but Edward was forced to fly from a palace to a foreign land. But as sudden changes of fortune are seldom permanent, Henry was at length thrown from the throne, and Edward restored to his place. And as always happens, the Parliament adhered to the party that seemed strongest.

title: Common Sense
input: Immediate necessity can render certain actions convenient, but if such actions continue unchecked, they may lead to oppression. It is important to distinguish between expedience and what is right. During the crises that America faced, the appointment of representatives from various Houses of Assembly was a practical and appropriate solution for consultation, and this approach helped to protect the continent from disaster. However, it is likely that a Congress will always be in existence, and it is essential for those invested in maintaining order to consider how its members are chosen. This raises a question for those who study human behavior: is it wise for a single group of individuals to hold both representation and election powers? As we plan for future generations, it is crucial to recognize that virtue is not something that can be inherited.
human: Immediate necessity makes many things convenient, which if continued would grow into oppressions. Expedience and right are different things. When the calamities of America required a consultation, there was no method so ready, or at that time so proper, as to appoint persons from the several Houses of Assembly for that purpose; and the wisdom with which they have proceeded hath preserved this continent from ruin. But as it is more than probable that we shall never be without a Congress, every well wisher to good order, must own, that the mode for choosing members of that body, deserves consideration. And I put it as a question to those, who make a study of mankind, whether representation and election is not too great a power for one and the same body of men to possess? When we are planning for posterity, we ought to remember, that virtue is not hereditary.
base: Immediate need can make some actions seem easy, but if they go on without check, they can become unfair. It’s key to tell the difference between what’s handy and what’s right. When America was in trouble, letting people from different groups pick leaders worked well and helped keep the country safe. But a Congress is probably always going to be there, so those who care about order must think about how its members are chosen. This brings up a question for those who study people: is it smart for one group to have both the power to choose and the power to represent? As we think about the future, we must remember that good character isn’t something you’re born with.
finetuned: But as immediate necessity makes some things convenient, and if continued without a check, becomes a tyranny; it becomes necessary to distinguish between Expedience and Right; and to inquire, Whether it is Expedient to make the Representatives of the several Houses of Assembly, to be consulted on all Cases, in which the United States have an interest, and which are not too trifling to be omitted. In the Cases of the great embarrassments which America sustained, this was a great and proper Expedient, and prevented the continent from being involved in the worst Consequences. But a Congress will always be in being, and those who have any Interest in the Publick Peace and Safety, must consider in what Manner the Members thereof are chosen. And it is the Question which all Philosophers ought to ask, Whether it is Expedient to give the same Body of Men, the Powers of Representation and Election? For as we are concerned in the Interest of our Posterity, we ought never to suppose that Virtue is to be inherited.

title: Common Sense
input:
It may be suggested that describing the constitution of England as a union of three powers that check each other may overlook some complexities, as this characterization might not fully capture the nuances involved. 

Firstly, it can often be argued that the monarchy may present a tendency towards seeking absolute power, which implies the necessity of oversight to ensure that such ambitions are kept in check. 

Secondly, there is a notion that the Commons, due to their appointment, may be viewed as more prudent or deserving of trust compared to the crown. 

In summary, the relationship among the powers within the English constitution is complex and may be subject to differing interpretations.
human:
To say that the constitution of England is a union of three powers reciprocally checking each other, is farcical, either the words have no meaning, or they are flat contradictions.

First. - That the king is not to be trusted without being looked after, or in other words, that a thirst for absolute power is the natural disease of monarchy.

Secondly. - That the commons, by being appointed for that purpose, are either wiser or more worthy of confidence than the crown.
base: The idea that the English constitution is a balance of three powers checking each other might miss some of the finer points. The monarchy could push for more power, so there needs to be a way to stop that. The Commons, because they’re chosen, might seem smarter or more trustworthy than the crown. The way the powers work in England is tricky and can be seen differently by people.
finetuned: There is perhaps a great deal of want of exactness in this expression of the constitution of England, as a union of three powers which check one another. First, because the monarchy is supposed to be disposed to ambition, and therefore to require a check. Secondly, because the commons, being the inferior body, are supposed to be more reasonable, and more entitled to credit, than the crown.

title: Common Sense
input: Human beings may have started as equals in the process of creation, and this equality could only have been altered by later circumstances. The differences between wealth and poverty can often be explained, perhaps without needing to resort to the more severe terms of oppression and greed. While oppression can frequently be a result of wealth disparities, it is rarely the direct cause of them. Additionally, while greed may help someone avoid severe financial hardship, it often makes them too cautious to achieve true wealth. In summary, the dynamics of equality and wealth are complex and influenced by various factors.
human: Mankind being originally equals in the order of creation, the equality could only be destroyed by some subsequent circumstance; the distinctions of rich, and poor, may in a great measure be accounted for, and that without having recourse to the harsh ill sounding names of oppression and avarice. Oppression is often the consequence, but seldom or never the means of riches; and though avarice will preserve a man from being necessitously poor, it generally makes him too timorous to be wealthy.
base: We started off equal, created by the same hand. That equality changed over time, shaped by what came after. The gap between rich and poor isn’t always about bad things like being forced to suffer or wanting more than you need. Oppression might come from being poor, but it doesn’t start the gap. Greed can help someone stay out of trouble, but it stops them from really getting ahead. So the story of fairness and money is complicated, with many parts to it.
finetuned: Man began equal, and this equality could only be altered by circumstances. The inequality of wealth and poverty, then, must have been brought into existence by circumstances. The inequality of wealth and poverty is easily explained, without resorting to the words oppression and greed. Oppression may often be the consequence of inequality, but it is rarely the cause. Greed may save from the extremities of poverty, but it makes its possessor too cautious to become rich.

title: Emma
input:
Emma found herself somewhat entertained by the idea that it was quite unusual and felt she had no defense for him. 

“I really cannot understand,” Mrs. Elton remarked, feeling the slight as any wife might, “how he could possibly do such a thing to you, of all people! You are certainly the last person one would think could be overlooked! My dear Mr. E., I am confident he must have left a message for you. Not even Knightley could be that forgetful; it must be that his servants overlooked it. I think that is likely the situation, especially with the Donwell staff, who, as I have frequently noted, can be rather clumsy and forgetful. I certainly would not allow someone like his Harry to serve at our sideboard for any reason. And regarding Mrs. Hodges, Wright does not hold her in high regard at all. She promised him a receipt but failed to send it.” 

In summary, Mrs. Elton conveys her disbelief at the situation and expresses her confidence that a misunderstanding has occurred due to the negligence of others.

And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright holds her very cheap indeed. - She promised Wright a receipt, and never sent it.”

title: Emma
input: Such a conclusion could not remain unaddressed by Mrs. Weston. She held Frank in high regard in nearly all aspects, and, moreover, she possessed a deep affection for him, which rendered her defense sincere. She articulated her points with considerable reason and an equal measure of affection; however, she had too many arguments to capture Emma’s attention effectively. Soon, Emma’s focus had shifted either to Brunswick Square or to Donwell, and she neglected to make an effort to listen. When Mrs. Weston concluded with the remark, “We have not yet received the letter for which we are so anxious, you know, but I hope it will arrive soon,” Emma found herself compelled to pause before responding and ultimately had to provide an answer at random, as she struggled to recall precisely which letter they were so eagerly anticipating.

title: Emma
input: Mr. Weston's happiness was clear and unmistakable. He was truly delighted, as this was exactly the situation he had hoped for. Now Frank would genuinely be part of their neighborhood. After all, what did nine miles mean to a young man? Just an hour's ride. He would be able to visit constantly. The difference between Richmond and London in this regard was enough to determine whether they would see him regularly or not at all. Sixteen miles—or even eighteen, since it was a full eighteen to Manchester Street—was a serious obstacle. Even if he managed to get away, the entire day would be consumed by traveling there and back. There was no comfort in having him in London; he might as well be at Enscombe. Richmond, however, was exactly the right distance for easy visits. This suggests that closer was not necessarily better.

title: Emma
input: “A man,” he remarked, “must possess a significantly high opinion of himself when he invites others to leave the comfort of their own fireside to face a day such as this for the purpose of visiting him. He must believe himself to be a most agreeable individual; I could not undertake such an action. It is the utmost absurdity—indeed, it is presently snowing!—to insist that individuals forsake their comfort at home, as well as the folly of individuals not choosing to remain comfortably at home when they have the opportunity to do so. If we were compelled to venture out on an evening like this due to any obligation or necessity, we would consider it a considerable hardship; yet here we are, likely clad in somewhat lighter garments than usual, proceeding voluntarily, without justification, in defiance of the instinct of nature, which advises humanity, through every sensory experience, to remain at home and shelter what they can. Here we are, preparing to spend five tedious hours in another individual’s residence, with nothing to discuss or hear that has not already been exchanged yesterday and may not be repeated tomorrow. We are venturing out in dismal weather, with the prospect of returning in even worse conditions; four horses and four servants have been summoned merely to transport five idle, shivering individuals into colder rooms and inferior company than they could have enjoyed at home.”
human: “A man,” said he, “must have a very good opinion of himself when he asks people to leave their own fireside, and encounter such a day as this, for the sake of coming to see him. He must think himself a most agreeable fellow; I could not do such a thing. It is the greatest absurdity - Actually snowing at this moment! - The folly of not allowing people to be comfortable at home - and the folly of people’s not staying comfortably at home when they can! If we were obliged to go out such an evening as this, by any call of duty or business, what a hardship we should deem it; - and here are we, probably with rather thinner clothing than usual, setting forward voluntarily, without excuse, in defiance of the voice of nature, which tells man, in every thing given to his view or his feelings, to stay at home himself, and keep all under shelter that he can; - here are we setting forward to spend five dull hours in another man’s house, with nothing to say or to hear that was not said and heard yesterday, and may not be said and heard again to-morrow. Going in dismal weather, to return probably in worse; - four horses and four servants taken out for nothing but to convey five idle, shivering creatures into colder rooms and worse company than they might have had at home.”

It’s absurd—really, it is—there’s snow falling! To tell people to leave their comfort and go out in the cold is foolish. If we had to go out because of some duty, we’d call it a hardship. But here we are, dressed in lighter clothes than usual, going out on our own, against nature’s advice. Nature tells us to stay inside and keep warm. We’re heading to someone else’s house to spend five hours talking about things we already discussed yesterday and might not even mention tomorrow. We’re going out in bad weather, and we might come back even worse off. Four horses and four servants have been brought just to take five of us into colder rooms and worse company than we could have had at home.”

title: Peter Pan
input:
After Mr. and Mrs. Darling departed the house, the night-lights beside the beds of the three children continued to glow brightly. They were particularly charming night-lights, and one might wish that the children could have stayed awake to see Peter. However, Wendy's light flickered and emitted a large yawn, which caused the other two lights to yawn as well. Before they could manage to stop, all three lights extinguished.

Now, a new light filled the room, a thousand times more brilliant than the night-lights. During the time it took to describe this, it had searched through all the drawers in the nursery, seeking Peter's shadow, rummaged through the wardrobe, and turned every pocket inside out. This was not a traditional light; it created illumination by moving rapidly. When it paused for a moment, one could see it was a fairy, no larger than a hand, yet still growing. Her name was Tinker Bell, and she was elegantly dressed in a skeleton leaf, tailored to showcase her figure effectively. She had a slight tendency toward being plump.
human:
For a moment after Mr. and Mrs. Darling left the house the night-lights by the beds of the three children continued to burn clearly. They were awfully nice little night-lights, and one cannot help wishing that they could have kept awake to see Peter; but Wendy’s light blinked and gave such a yawn that the other two yawned also, and before they could close their mouths all the three went out.

There was another light in the room now, a thousand times brighter than the night-lights, and in the time we have taken to say this, it had been in all the drawers in the nursery, looking for Peter’s shadow, rummaged the wardrobe and turned every pocket inside out. It was not really a light; it made this light by flashing about so quickly, but when it came to rest for a second you saw it was a fairy, no longer than your hand, but still growing. It was a girl called Tinker Bell exquisitely gowned in a skeleton leaf, cut low and square, through which her figure could be seen to the best advantage. She was slightly inclined to embonpoint.

title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

We heard the door open, a few hurried words, and then quick steps on the linoleum. Our own door flew open, and a lady entered the room, dressed in some dark-coloured fabric and wearing a black veil.

She said it was very kind of us to come, and urged the visitor to have some wine and water, to sit comfortably, and to tell us all about it. She also asked whether the visitor would prefer that she send James off to bed.

This was not the first time she had spoken to us about her husband's trouble, to me as a doctor and to my wife as an old friend and school companion. We soothed and comforted her as best we could with the words we could find. We asked whether she knew where her husband was, and whether it might be possible for us to bring him back to her. This highlights how she relied on both professional and personal support in a time of distress.

He took a sovereign from his pocket and placed it on the table, turning away as if his discontent was too profound for expression. A few moments later, he paused under a lamp-post and laughed in a silent manner characteristic of him.

He noted that a man with distinctive whiskers and the "Pink ’un" newspaper visible from his pocket could easily be persuaded to share information through a wager. He suggested that if he had offered the man £100 directly, he would not have provided as thorough information as he did when prompted by the notion of a bet. Holmes then indicated that they were likely close to concluding their investigation, with only the decision remaining about whether to visit Mrs. Oakshott that evening or to postpone until the following day. He observed that the response from the unfriendly man implied that there were others, in addition to themselves, who were concerned about the situation.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: Humans often exhibit timidity and a sense of apology; they no longer stand tall. They hesitate to assert, "I think," or "I am," instead relying on the words of saints or sages. They feel embarrassment in the presence of a blade of grass or a blooming rose. The roses outside my window do not refer to past blooms or to those of better quality; they exist simply as they are, in unity with the divine in the present moment. Time holds no significance for them. There exists only the rose, perfect in each instance of its being. Before a leaf bud unfurls, its entire life is already at play. In the fully blossomed flower, nothing more exists, while in the leafless root, nothing less is found. Its essence is fulfilled, and it fulfills nature in every moment alike. In contrast, humans tend to delay or reminisce. They fail to engage with the present, often looking back with regret or, distracted by their surroundings, stretch forward to anticipate the future. They cannot achieve happiness or strength until they learn to embrace the present, living in harmony with nature beyond the constraints of time.
human: Man is timid and apologetic; he is no longer upright; he dares not say "I think," "I am," but quotes some saint or sage. He is ashamed before the blade of grass or the blowing rose. These roses under my window make no reference to former roses or to better ones; they are for what they are; they exist with God to-day. There is no time to them. There is simply the rose; it is perfect in every moment of its existence. Before a leaf-bud has burst, its whole life acts; in the full-blown flower there is no more; in the leafless root there is no less. Its nature is satisfied, and it satisfies nature, in all moments alike. But man postpones, or remembers; he does not live in the present, but with a reverted eye laments the past, or, heedless of the riches that surround him, stands on tiptoe to foresee the future. He cannot be happy and strong until he too lives with nature in the present, above time.

They can’t be happy or strong until they learn to live in the present, in harmony with nature beyond time.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: You may find yourself admiring this tower of granite, which has withstood the challenges of many ages. However, it is worth considering that this impressive structure was constructed by a small, skilled hand, suggesting that the creator may hold more significance than the creation itself. The hand that built the tower can often dismantle it even more swiftly. Perhaps more important than the hand is the unseen thought that guided its construction; behind every rough outcome, there tends to be a finer cause. When examined closely, what we perceive as permanent might reveal its underlying secrets. For instance, a considerable estate might seem like a solid and enduring fact to women and children, yet to a merchant, it may appear as something easily formed from various materials and just as easily lost. An orchard, well-tended land, and favorable conditions may seem like fixed assets to a city dweller, but to a larger farmer, they are often as changeable as the harvest. Nature may give the impression of stability, but it too has causes that can be understood, leading one to question whether these expansive fields and distinctive leaves truly remain so unchanging. The concept of permanence can vary in meaning. Everything exists in a state of flux. Just as moons do not limit spiritual power, neither do other tangible objects.
human: You admire this tower of granite, weathering the hurts of so many ages. Yet a little waving hand built this huge wall, and that which builds is better than that which is built. The hand that built can topple it down much faster. Better than the hand and nimbler was the invisible thought which wrought through it; and thus ever, behind the coarse effect, is a fine cause, which, being narrowly seen, is itself the effect of a finer cause. Everything looks permanent until its secret is known. A rich estate appears to women and children a firm and lasting fact; to a merchant, one easily created out of any materials, and easily lost. An orchard, good tillage, good grounds, seem a fixture, like a gold mine, or a river, to a citizen; but to a large farmer, not much more fixed than the state of the crop. Nature looks provokingly stable and secular, but it has a cause like all the rest; and when once I comprehend that, will these fields stretch so immovably wide, these leaves hang so individually considerable? Permanence is a word of degrees. Every thing is medial. Moons are no more bounds to spiritual power than bat-balls.

That hand might be more important than the tower itself. The same hand that made the tower can take it down just as easily. Maybe more than the hand, it’s the idea that was in the mind when it was built that matters. Behind every rough thing, there’s a more subtle reason. If you look closely, what looks solid might have hidden truths. For example, a big house might seem like something strong and lasting to kids and women, but to a merchant, it’s just made of different things and can be lost just as fast. A well-kept orchard and good land might seem like something fixed to a city person, but to a bigger farmer, they’re as changeable as the harvest. Nature looks steady, but it has reasons too. That makes you wonder if those big fields and pretty leaves really never change. Permanence means different things. Everything is always changing. Just like moons don’t stop spiritual power, nothing else stays the same.

But then, this imposing pile was made by a small and dexterous hand; and the hand, perhaps, is more to be wondered at than the handiwork. The hand which made the tower can make it fall again, in a few moments. Perhaps the hand, after all, is not the most important thing; behind every rough effect there is a finer cause. If you look closely, you will find what you call fixed and permanent to be a secret. An orchard, good land, and good season, seem to the city dweller to be fixed and permanent; but to a greater farmer, as easily formed and as easily lost. Nature seems to you to be permanent; but she has causes, too, and you may find them out; and will you not then wonder whether these broad fields and these peculiar leaves are really as permanent as you think? Permanence is a word that has many meanings. Everything is in a state of flux. Moons do not bar the way to the spiritual power; neither do other things.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: People may think that when you reject popular standards, you are rejecting all standards and simply embracing lawlessness; and a bold, pleasure-seeking person may use the name of philosophy to make his crimes seem respectable. But the law of consciousness remains. There are two confessionals, and in one or the other we must be absolved. You may complete your round of duties by clearing yourself in the direct way or in the reflective way. Consider whether you have satisfied your relations to father, mother, cousin, neighbor, town, cat, and dog; whether any of these can rightly blame you. But I may also neglect this reflective standard and absolve myself to myself. I have my own strict claims and my own complete circle. It denies the name of duty to many offices that are called duties. Yet if I can pay its debts, it allows me to dispense with the popular code. If anyone imagines that this law is lax, let him keep its commandment for one day. In short, while others may mistake self-rule for lawlessness, the law of consciousness still holds, and it can either replace or confirm the ordinary code depending on how faithfully we meet its demands.

But the law of consciousness abides. There are two confessionals, in one or the other of which we must be shriven. You may fulfill your round of duties by clearing yourself in the direct, or in the reflex way. Consider whether you have satisfied your relations to father, mother, cousin, neighbor, town, cat, and dog; whether any of these can upbraid you. But I may also neglect this reflex standard, and absolve me to myself. I have my own stern claims and perfect circle. It denies the name of duty to many offices that are called duties. But if I can discharge its debts, it enables me to dispense with the popular code. If any one imagines that this law is lax, let him keep its commandment one day.

A bold, pleasure-seeking person might use philosophy to make their bad behavior sound good. But the law of consciousness is still there. There are two confessionals, and we have to be forgiven in one or the other. You can clear your name directly or by thinking about it. Ask yourself if you've treated your father, mother, cousin, neighbor, town, cat, and dog right. Do any of them have a reason to blame you? I might also skip this thinking and forgive myself. I have my own rules and my own set of people. It doesn't call many things duty that are called duties. But if I can meet those rules, I can ignore the usual rules. If someone thinks this law is easy, let them follow it for a day. In short, while others see self-rule as lawlessness, the law of consciousness still exists. It can take the place of or support the usual rules, depending on how well we follow it.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: We require books that possess this profound cathartic quality far more than we require books focused on political science or private economics. Life presents itself as a celebration solely to the wise. When viewed from the perspective of prudence, it reveals a tattered and perilous facade. The transgressions against the laws of nature committed by both our predecessors and contemporaries result in consequences that affect us as well. The presence of disease and deformity in our environment serves as a testament to the violations of natural, intellectual, and moral laws, often compounding these violations to generate pervasive suffering. Conditions such as tetanus that contorts an individual’s posture, rabies that induces irrational behavior towards loved ones, and madness that leads to bizarre eating habits—along with war, plague, cholera, and famine—reflect a certain brutality inherent in nature. This brutality, having originated from human wrongdoing, must manifest itself through human suffering. Unfortunately, it is noteworthy that nearly every individual has, to some degree, become a participant in this collective wrongdoing, thereby rendering themselves liable for a share in the subsequent atonement.
human: 3. We need books of this tart cathartic virtue, more than books of political science, or of private economy. Life is a festival only to the wise. Seen from the nook and chimney-side of prudence, it wears a ragged and dangerous front. The violations of the laws of nature by our predecessors and our contemporaries are punished in us also. The disease and deformity around us certify the infraction of natural, intellectual, and moral laws, and often violation on violation to breed such compound misery. A lockjaw that bends a man's head back to his heels, hydrophobia that makes him bark at his wife and babes, insanity that makes him eat grass; war, plague, cholera, famine indicate a certain ferocity in nature, which, as it had its inlet by human crime, must have its outlet by human suffering. Unhappily, almost no man exists who has not in his own person become, to some amount, a stockholder in the sin, and so made himself liable to a share in the expiation.

The mistakes people before and now have made against nature’s rules affect us too. Disease and bad looks around us show how people have broken natural, smart, and moral rules. These breaks make more suffering. Things like tetanus that twist someone’s body, rabies that makes people act strangely towards family, madness that leads to odd eating—plus war, plague, cholera, and famine—show nature’s rough side. This roughness came from people’s bad actions, so it must come through people’s pain. Sadly, most people have done some of this wrong, so they’re part of the trouble and must face some of the punishment.
finetuned: We want books of this sort far more than books of political science or of private economics. Life is a festival only to the wise. To prudence it is a ragged and dangerous mask. The crimes against the laws of nature committed by our ancestors and our contemporaries, have their due of effect upon us. Disease and deformity in our neighbourhood are evidence of crimes against the laws of nature, of the laws of intellect and of the laws of morals, and these crimes multiplied and compounded together produce a universal suffering. Tetanus, which twists the body into a most grotesque attitude; rabies, which turns the mind against the flesh, and the flesh against the mind, and the flesh against the mind; madness, which makes the man eat the flesh of his own body; war, plague, cholera, and famine - these are the signs of a certain brutal nature. This brutal nature having proceeded from man’s crime, must be satisfied with the suffering of man. And it is no small thing to observe, that nearly every man has, to some extent, become a participant in the crime, and is therefore liable to his share in the expiation.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
input:
Upon arriving home, he noticed that his servant was still awake, waiting for him. He instructed the servant to rest and then settled onto the sofa in the library, reflecting on some of the remarks made by Lord Henry. 

He began to question whether it was indeed true that one could never change. A deep yearning for the innocence of his youth surfaced—his pure, unblemished boyhood, as Lord Henry had referred to it. He was aware that he had compromised himself, allowing corruption to infiltrate his thoughts and instilling a sense of horror in his imagination; he recognized that he had negatively influenced others and had taken a troubling pleasure in doing so. Among the lives he had interacted with, it was those with the greatest potential that he had led to disappointment. Yet, he wondered if all was lost. Was there no possibility for redemption?
human:
When he reached home, he found his servant waiting up for him. He sent him to bed, and threw himself down on the sofa in the library, and began to think over some of the things that Lord Henry had said to him.

Was it really true that one could never change? He felt a wild longing for the unstained purity of his boyhood - his rose-white boyhood, as Lord Henry had once called it. He knew that he had tarnished himself, filled his mind with corruption and given horror to his fancy; that he had been an evil influence to others, and had experienced a terrible joy in being so; and that of the lives that had crossed his own, it had been the fairest and the most full of promise that he had brought to shame. But was it all irretrievable? Was there no hope for him?
base: He came home and saw his servant still up, waiting. He told the servant to go to bed and sat on the sofa in the library, thinking about what Lord Henry had said. He started wondering if really, you could never change. A feeling came over him for the innocence of his young days—the pure, clean boyhood Lord Henry had called it. He knew he had let things slide, let corruption creep into his mind and made his thoughts scary. He knew he had hurt others, that he had enjoyed making them sad. Among the people he had met, it was the ones with the most promise he had let down. Yet he wondered if everything was gone. Could there be any way to make it right?
finetuned: On reaching home he found that his servant was still awake, waiting for him. He told him to go to bed, and then sat down on the sofa in the library and thought over some of the things which Lord Henry had said. “Was it true,” he asked himself, “that one could never change? Did I really mean to be what I was? Did I really want to be what I was? Oh, my poor innocent boyhood! my pure, my clean, my untouched boyhood! I have been degraded! I have been corrupted! I have been horror-struck! I have been an evil influence! I have been evil to others! I have been evil to those whom I have influenced! I have been evil to those who had the most promise! But is there no salvation? Is there no hope?”

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
input: The worship of the senses has often been criticized, as many people instinctively fear passions and sensations that seem more powerful than themselves, sensations shared with less complex forms of life. However, Dorian Gray believed that the true essence of the senses had not been fully grasped. He thought they had remained primitive and animalistic because society attempted to suppress or punish them, rather than nurturing them as components of a new spirituality characterized by an appreciation for beauty. Reflecting on humanity's journey through history, he felt a profound sense of loss. Much had been sacrificed with little benefit, leading to extreme rejection of pleasure and painful self-denial. These responses stemmed from fear and resulted in a degradation that was far worse than the imagined decline they sought to avoid. Nature, in its ironic way, drove the ascetic into the wild, providing him with animals as companions instead of fellow humans.
human: The worship of the senses has often, and with much justice, been decried, men feeling a natural instinct of terror about passions and sensations that seem stronger than themselves, and that they are conscious of sharing with the less highly organized forms of existence. But it appeared to Dorian Gray that the true nature of the senses had never been understood, and that they had remained savage and animal merely because the world had sought to starve them into submission or to kill them by pain, instead of aiming at making them elements of a new spirituality, of which a fine instinct for beauty was to be the dominant characteristic. As he looked back upon man moving through history, he was haunted by a feeling of loss. So much had been surrendered! and to such little purpose! There had been mad wilful rejections, monstrous forms of self-torture and self-denial, whose origin was fear and whose result was a degradation infinitely more terrible than that fancied degradation from which, in their ignorance, they had sought to escape; Nature, in her wonderful irony, driving out the anchorite to feed with the wild animals of the desert and giving to the hermit the beasts of the field as his companions.
base: The worship of the senses has been criticized often. People fear passions and sensations that feel stronger than themselves, things shared with simpler lives. Dorian Gray thought the real nature of the senses wasn't fully understood. He believed they stayed basic and animal-like because society tried to stop them, not help them grow into something new, a kind of spirit that values beauty. Looking at history, he felt a deep loss. A lot was given up with little gain, leading to extreme rejection of pleasure and hard self-denial. These reactions came from fear and caused a downfall worse than what they tried to avoid. Nature, in its way, pushed the ascetic into the wild, giving him animals as friends instead of people.
finetuned: The worship of the senses had always been blamed, for men had instinctively shuddered before passions and sensations more powerful than themselves, sensations common to the lower creatures. But Dorian Gray did not believe that the real soul of the senses had ever been discovered. He thought that they had remained beastly and beastlike because society had tried to destroy or chastise them instead of cultivating them as part of a new and terrible religion, a religion in which beauty was adored. Humanity had gone through history, he thought, and had suffered so much for so little. So much had been given for so little, that men had come to hate pleasure with a hatred that was almost extreme, and to suffer with a suffering that was almost painful, from fear. Fear had driven the ascetic into the wilds of the world, and given him for companions the animals instead of the human race.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
input:
"Your life seems quite troubling, full of challenges that may have led you down a difficult path. It appears that your journey has culminated in some serious decisions. As I consider my next steps, it’s not your life that occupies my thoughts."

"Ah, Alan," Dorian replied softly with a sigh, "I wish you could feel even a small fraction of the compassion for me that I feel for you." He then turned his gaze toward the garden. Campbell remained silent in response.
human:
“Your life? Good heavens! what a life that is! You have gone from corruption to corruption, and now you have culminated in crime. In doing what I am going to do - what you force me to do - it is not of your life that I am thinking.”

“Ah, Alan,” murmured Dorian with a sigh, “I wish you had a thousandth part of the pity for me that I have for you.” He turned away as he spoke and stood looking out at the garden. Campbell made no answer.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
input:
When a highly respected physician, who also happens to be one's husband, tells friends and family that there is likely nothing wrong except for a temporary bout of nervous depression and a minor tendency toward hysteria, it leaves one in a difficult position. 

My brother, who is also a physician of similar reputation, shares the same opinion.

As a result, I am advised to take phosphates or phosphites—whichever it may be—along with tonics, travel, fresh air, and exercise, while being strongly discouraged from engaging in any work until I feel better. In summary, the situation involves navigating the recommendations of trusted medical professionals while managing personal health concerns.
human:
If a physician of high standing, and one’s own husband, assures friends and relatives that there is really nothing the matter with one but temporary nervous depression - a slight hysterical tendency - what is one to do?

My brother is also a physician, and also of high standing, and he says the same thing.

So I take phosphates or phosphites - whichever it is, and tonics, and journeys, and air, and exercise, and am absolutely forbidden to “work” until I am well again.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
input:
It is rare for ordinary individuals such as John and me to acquire ancestral homes for the summer. 

A colonial mansion, a hereditary estate, or even a haunted house would be a delightful notion, yet that may be too much to hope for. 

If it were not, why would it be rented at such a low price? Additionally, why has it remained unoccupied for so long? 

John is exceedingly practical. He lacks patience for faith, harbors a strong aversion to superstition, and openly mocks any discussions of concepts that cannot be experienced through the senses or quantified.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
input:
John has never seemed nervous in his life. He finds amusement in my reaction to the wallpaper. 

Initially, he planned to replace it, but later he suggested that I was allowing it to dominate my thoughts. He asserted that for someone with a nervous disposition, indulging such whims is detrimental.

He explained that if the wallpaper were removed, I would then focus on the heavy bedstead, followed by the barred windows, and ultimately the gate at the top of the stairs, and so forth.
human:
I suppose John never was nervous in his life. He laughs at me so about this wallpaper!

At first he meant to repaper the room, but afterwards he said that I was letting it get the better of me, and that nothing was worse for a nervous patient than to give way to such fancies.

He said that after the wallpaper was changed it would be the heavy bedstead, and then the barred windows, and then that gate at the head of the stairs, and so on.

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input: As we prepared to sign the aforementioned articles, which would bind us and our heirs for fifty years, Mr. Brockden, the scrivener, addressed us. He noted, "You are young men, but it is unlikely that any of you will live to see the end of the term established in the document." Despite his assertion, several of us are still living today. However, the instrument was rendered void just a few years later due to a charter that incorporated the company and granted it perpetual status.

A number of us, however, are yet living; but the instrument was after a few years rendered null by a charter that incorporated and gave perpetuity to the company.

He said, "You are young men, but it's not likely any of you will live to see the end of the term in the document." Even so, some of us are still alive today. But the document was canceled just a few years later because a charter was issued that set up the company and gave it forever.

But the instrument was rendered void within a few years after, by a charter which incorporated the company and gave it a perpetual term.

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input: Mr. Logan, who adhered to the Quaker faith, wrote an address in support of defensive war, providing several strong arguments for his stance. He entrusted me with sixty pounds to be invested in lottery tickets for the battery, with instructions for any prizes to be dedicated solely to that purpose. He shared an anecdote about his former employer, William Penn, regarding the topic of defense. As a young man, Penn traveled from England with his proprietary and served as their secretary during a time of war. Their ship was pursued by an armed vessel believed to be an enemy. The captain prepared for defense but informed Penn and the Quakers that their assistance was not anticipated, encouraging them to retreat to the cabin. However, James Logan chose to remain on deck and took his position by a gun. Ultimately, the supposed enemy turned out to be an ally, and no conflict ensued. When Logan returned below deck to share this information, Penn reprimanded him for remaining on deck and participating in defense, citing the principles of Friends and that such action had not been requested by the captain. This rebuke, delivered in front of others, irritated Logan, who responded, "As your servant, why did you not command me to come down? It seemed you were content for me to help defend the ship when you perceived danger."
human: The honorable and learned Mr. Logan, who had always been of that sect, was one who wrote an address to them, declaring his approbation of defensive war, and supporting his opinion by many strong arguments. He put into my hands sixty pounds to be laid out in lottery tickets for the battery, with directions to apply what prizes might be drawn wholly to that service. He told me the following anecdote of his old master, William Penn, respecting defense. He came over from England, when a young man, with that proprietary, and as his secretary. It was war-time, and their ship was chas'd by an armed vessel, suppos'd to be an enemy. Their captain prepar'd for defense; but told William Penn, and his company of Quakers, that he did not expect their assistance, and they might retire into the cabin, which they did, except James Logan, who chose to stay upon deck, and was quarter'd to a gun. The suppos'd enemy prov'd a friend, so there was no fighting; but when the secretary went down to communicate the intelligence, William Penn rebuk'd him severely for staying upon deck, and undertaking to assist in defending the vessel, contrary to the principles of Friends, especially as it had not been required by the captain. This reproof, being before all the company, piqu'd the secretary, who answer'd, "I being thy servant, why did thee not order me to come down? But thee was willing enough that I should stay and help to fight the ship when thee thought there was danger."

The rebuke, in front of others, made Logan angry. He said, “As your servant, why didn’t you tell me to come down? It seemed you were happy for me to help defend the ship when you saw danger.”

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input: I stayed there for nearly three months, and by that time I could count among my new friends Judge Allen, Samuel Bustill, the secretary of the Province, Isaac Pearson, Joseph Cooper, and several members of the Smith family who were in the Assembly, as well as Isaac Decow, the surveyor-general. The latter was a shrewd and wise old man who told me that he had started out on his own when he was young by hauling clay for brick-makers, learned to write after he had reached adulthood, carried the chain for surveyors who then taught him surveying, and had now, through his own hard work, acquired a comfortable estate. He said to me, "I foresee that you will soon take this man's business away from him and make a fortune in it at Philadelphia." At that time he had no idea at all that I intended to set up there or anywhere else. These friends were later very helpful to me, just as I was occasionally helpful to some of them, and they all continued to think well of me for as long as they lived.

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input:
This year, my responsibilities with the post-office led me to take a journey to New England. During this trip, the College of Cambridge, acting independently, awarded me the degree of Master of Arts. Prior to that, Yale College in Connecticut had offered me a similar honor. As a result, I received these distinctions without formally studying at either institution. It seems they were granted in recognition of my contributions and discoveries in the field of electricity within natural philosophy.

In 1754, with the possibility of war with France looming again, a congress of representatives from various colonies was summoned by the Lords of Trade to meet in Albany. The purpose of this gathering was to discuss strategies for defending both our land and theirs with the leaders of the Six Nations. Upon receiving this order, Governor Hamilton informed the House and requested that they provide suitable gifts for the Native American leaders for this occasion. He proposed that the speaker, Mr. Norris, and I join Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters as commissioners representing Pennsylvania. The House approved this nomination and arranged for the gifts, although they were somewhat hesitant about engaging outside the provinces. We convened with the other commissioners in Albany around mid-June.

Yale College, in Connecticut, had before made me a similar compliment. Thus, without studying in any college, I came to partake of their honours. They were conferr'd in consideration of my improvements and discoveries in the electric branch of natural philosophy.

In 1754, war with France being again apprehended, a congress of commissioners from the different colonies was, by an order of the Lords of Trade, to be assembled at Albany, there to confer with the chiefs of the Six Nations concerning the means of defending both their country and ours. Governor Hamilton, having receiv'd this order, acquainted the House with it, requesting they would furnish proper presents for the Indians, to be given on this occasion; and naming the speaker (Mr. Norris) and myself to join Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters as commissioners to act for Pennsylvania. The House approv'd the nomination, and provided the goods for the present, and tho' they did not much like treating out of the provinces; and we met the other commissioners at Albany about the middle of June.

He asked the House to send Mr. Norris and me with Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Peters as Pennsylvania's reps. The House said yes, but they weren't sure about sending people outside the provinces. We met the other commissioners in Albany in mid-June.

This year, the post-office having occasioned me to make a journey to New England, the College of Cambridge, independently of me, gave me the degree of Master of Arts; and before that, the Yale College of Connecticut, gave me the same. I therefore received these distinctions, without studying either of them. It was in acknowledgment of my services and discoveries in the philosophy of electricity.

In the year 1754, the danger of war with France again appearing, a congress of representatives of different colonies was called by the Lords of Trade, to assemble at Albany, for the purpose of deliberating with the governors of our country and of theirs, on the means of defending their lands and ours, with the leaders of the Six Nations. Upon this order, Governor Hamilton informed the House, and desired that they would furnish the Native American leaders with proper presents for this occasion. He offered himself, with Mr. Norris, and I, as a commission for Pennsylvania, to be sent with Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters. The House approved the nomination, and arranged the presents, though they were unwilling to go out of the provinces. We met the other commissioners at Albany in the middle of June.

title: Walden
input: It may seem to some people that earlier generations have already covered the whole ground of human life, both the heights and the valleys, and that everything has been taken care of. According to Evelyn, “the wise Solomon prescribed ordinances for the very distances of trees; and the Roman prætors have decided how often you may go into your neighbor’s land to gather the acorns which fall on it without trespass, and what share belongs to that neighbor.” Hippocrates, it seems, even left directions on how we should cut our nails—that is, even with the ends of the fingers, neither shorter nor longer. Without a doubt, the very tedium and boredom that claim to have exhausted life’s variety and joys are as old as Adam. But human capacities have never really been measured, and we should not judge what a person can do by precedents, since so little has been tried. Whatever your failures may have been up to now, “be not afflicted, my child, for who shall assign to thee what thou hast left undone?” In short, past examples may tell us less than we think about what remains possible for us.
