title: Walden
input: It is worth noting that my extensive engagement with beans constituted a unique experience, encompassing the processes of planting, hoeing, harvesting, threshing, and ultimately selling them; the latter task proved to be the most challenging of all, although I may add that tasting the beans also formed a part of my endeavor. My resolve to understand beans was unwavering. During their growth, I would hoe from five o’clock in the morning until noon and typically spent the remainder of the day attending to other responsibilities. Furthermore, one must consider the profound and intricate familiarity one develops with various types of weeds; this aspect merits some elaboration, as the labor involved was certainly repetitive. I ruthlessly disrupted their delicate structures, making stark distinctions with my hoe, leveling entire rows of one species while meticulously cultivating another. That is Roman wormwood; that is pigweed; that is sorrel; that is piper-grass—one must engage with them, sever their roots from the earth, exposing them to the sun, as any remaining fiber in the shade enables them to revert, becoming as verdant as a leek within two days. It was a prolonged struggle, not against cranes but rather against weeds, those persistent adversaries that enjoyed the advantages of sun, rain, and dew. Daily, the beans witnessed my arrival as I came to their defense, armed with a hoe, systematically thinning the ranks of their foes and filling the trenches with the fallen weeds. Many a formidable Hector, towering a full foot above his fellow competitors, succumbed to my efforts and lay defeated in the dust.
human: It was a singular experience that long acquaintance which I cultivated with beans, what with planting, and hoeing, and harvesting, and threshing, and picking over and selling them, - the last was the hardest of all, - I might add eating, for I did taste. I was determined to know beans. When they were growing, I used to hoe from five o’clock in the morning till noon, and commonly spent the rest of the day about other affairs. Consider the intimate and curious acquaintance one makes with various kinds of weeds, - it will bear some iteration in the account, for there was no little iteration in the labor, - disturbing their delicate organizations so ruthlessly, and making such invidious distinctions with his hoe, levelling whole ranks of one species, and sedulously cultivating another. That’s Roman wormwood, - that’s pigweed, - that’s sorrel, - that’s piper-grass, - have at him, chop him up, turn his roots upward to the sun, don’t let him have a fibre in the shade, if you do he’ll turn himself t’other side up and be as green as a leek in two days. A long war, not with cranes, but with weeds, those Trojans who had sun and rain and dews on their side. Daily the beans saw me come to their rescue armed with a hoe, and thin the ranks of their enemies, filling up the trenches with weedy dead. Many a lusty crest-waving Hector, that towered a whole foot above his crowding comrades, fell before my weapon and rolled in the dust.
base: My time with beans was unique. I planted, hoes, harvested, threshed, and sold them. Selling was the hardest part, though I should mention I also tasted the beans. I was determined to understand beans. While they grew, I hoes from five in the morning until noon, then did other things. Weeds were a big part of it. I had to know them all. I destroyed their roots, exposing them to the sun. Any left in the shade would grow again, like a leek in two days. It was a long fight, not against cranes but weeds. They had sun, rain, dew. Every day I came to defend the beans, hoes in hand, thinning their enemies. Many big weeds, a foot tall, fell to my efforts and lay in the dust.
finetuned: It was a long time, however, that I was so long engaged with beans. I planted them, I hoe’d them, I harvest’d them, I thresh’d them, I sold them; the last task was the most disagreeable, though I may add that I tasted them too. I had determined to know beans, and I did know them. While they grew, I hoe’d from five o’clock in the morning till noon, and usually till the rest of the day, if I was not employed in other matters. One must also remember the acquaintance one makes with all sorts of weeds, in their most abstruse and minute details; and this, perhaps, requires some explanation, for it was certainly monotonous. I destroyed their delicate structure with a ruthless hand, made a stark distinction with my hoe, levelled entire rows of one species, and cultivated another with the utmost care. That is Roman wormwood; that is pigweed; that is sorrel; that is piper-grass - one must have them, pull their roots out of the earth, and expose them to the sun, for any fibre that is left in the shade will make them revive in two days as green as a leek. It was a long fight, not with cranes, but with weeds, those ever-persistent foes, who had the advantages of sun, rain, and dew. Every day the beans saw me come to their defence with a hoe, thinning the ranks of their enemies, and filling the trenches with the fallen weeds. Many a fierce Hector, a foot in height above his fellow contestants, was brought low by my efforts, and lay prostrate in the dust.

title: Walden
input:
At midnight, when the moon illuminated the surroundings, I occasionally encountered hounds along my path, quietly prowling through the woods. These creatures would retreat into the underbrush, as if in fear, remaining still and silent until I had passed by.

Furthermore, squirrels and wild mice engaged in disputes over my collection of nuts. Surrounding my residence were numerous pitch pines, measuring from one to four inches in diameter, which had been gnawed by mice during the previous winter—a winter that was particularly harsh for them, as the snow lay deeply and persistently, compelling them to incorporate a significant amount of pine bark into their diet. Despite being entirely girdled, these trees appeared to thrive during the height of summer, with many having grown an entire foot. However, following another winter, these specimens were invariably found to be dead. It is noteworthy that a single mouse is permitted to consume an entire pine tree for its meal, gnawing around the trunk rather than vertically; perhaps this behavior is essential for thinning the densely growing trees.

Squirrels and wild mice disputed for my store of nuts. There were scores of pitch-pines around my house, from one to four inches in diameter, which had been gnawed by mice the previous winter, - a Norwegian winter for them, for the snow lay long and deep, and they were obliged to mix a large proportion of pine bark with their other diet. These trees were alive and apparently flourishing at mid-summer, and many of them had grown a foot, though completely girdled; but after another winter such were without exception dead. It is remarkable that a single mouse should thus be allowed a whole pine tree for its dinner, gnawing round instead of up and down it; but perhaps it is necessary in order to thin these trees, which are wont to grow up densely.

title: Walden
input: I observe the flow of morning cars with a sense of familiarity similar to that of watching the sun rise, which can often feel just as predictable. The trails of clouds stretching behind and ascending higher may briefly obscure the sun, casting my distant field into shadow, while the cars make their way to Boston. This celestial display can seem to diminish the significance of the earthly train of cars. The caretaker of the locomotive was up early on this winter morning, illuminated by starlight in the mountains, attending to his duties. Fire was stirred awake at this early hour to provide the necessary warmth and prepare the engine for its journey. If only the endeavor were as innocent as it is timely! When snow covers the ground, they may equip the engine with snow shoes and utilize a powerful plow to clear a path from the mountains to the coast, through which the cars, like a trailing drill, distribute restless passengers and goods across the nation. Throughout the day, the locomotive travels over the landscape, pausing only to allow its operator a rest. I sometimes find myself awakened at midnight by the engine’s heavy footsteps and forceful snorts, as it faces the harsh elements in a secluded forest, and it may only return to its station with the morning star, ready to embark on another journey without pause. Alternatively, I might hear it in the evening, releasing excess energy in its stable to relax before a few hours of rest. If only this endeavor were as noble and commanding as it is relentless and tireless!
human: I watch the passage of the morning cars with the same feeling that I do the rising of the sun, which is hardly more regular. Their train of clouds stretching far behind and rising higher and higher, going to heaven while the cars are going to Boston, conceals the sun for a minute and casts my distant field into the shade, a celestial train beside which the petty train of cars which hugs the earth is but the barb of the spear. The stabler of the iron horse was up early this winter morning by the light of the stars amid the mountains, to fodder and harness his steed. Fire, too, was awakened thus early to put the vital heat in him and get him off. If the enterprise were as innocent as it is early! If the snow lies deep, they strap on his snow-shoes, and with the giant plow, plow a furrow from the mountains to the seaboard, in which the cars, like a following drill-barrow, sprinkle all the restless men and floating merchandise in the country for seed. All day the fire-steed flies over the country, stopping only that his master may rest, and I am awakened by his tramp and defiant snort at midnight, when in some remote glen in the woods he fronts the elements incased in ice and snow; and he will reach his stall only with the morning star, to start once more on his travels without rest or slumber. Or perchance, at evening, I hear him in his stable blowing off the superfluous energy of the day, that he may calm his nerves and cool his liver and brain for a few hours of iron slumber. If the enterprise were as heroic and commanding as it is protracted and unwearied!

The clouds trail behind, rising higher, sometimes blocking the sun for a moment, casting my field into shadow while the cars head toward Boston. This sky scene makes the cars seem less important. The train engineer got up early on this winter morning, lit by mountain stars, doing his job. Fire was started to keep warm and ready the engine for the trip. If only this work were as simple as it is timely! When snow is on the ground, they put on snow shoes and use a big plow to clear a path from the mountains to the coast, where the cars, like a trailing drill, move restless people and goods across the country. All day, the engine moves over the land, stopping only to let the driver rest. I sometimes wake up at midnight to the engine’s heavy steps and loud noises as it faces the cold in a forest, and it returns to its station with the morning star, ready for another trip. Or I might hear it in the evening, letting out energy in the stable before a few hours of rest. If only this work were as noble as it is never-ending!

The fireman was up early on this winter morning, and with starlight in the mountains, was getting his duties done. Fire was stirred up at that early hour to give warmth, and prepare the engine for the trip. If only this endeavor were as innocent as it is timely! When the snow is on the ground they may put on snow shoes to the engine and use a plow to cut a way from the mountains to the coast, and the cars, like a trailing drill, spread the restless passengers and goods over the country. The locomotive goes all day over the country, stopping only to give the driver a rest. I sometimes wake up at midnight by the engine’s heavy footfalls and heavy snorts, and it is facing the wilderness in a forest, and it can only come back to its station with the morning star, and start on another journey without a stop. Or I may hear it in the evening, expending its surplus energy in the stable, and then to get ready for a few hours’ rest. If only this endeavor were as noble and commanding as it is relentless and tireless!

title: Walden
input: The indescribable innocence and benevolence of Nature, encompassing the sun, wind, and rain, as well as the seasons of summer and winter, provide an enduring sense of health and joy. Additionally, the deep connection that exists between Nature and humanity is so profound that, were any individual to experience genuine sorrow for justifiable reasons, the entirety of Nature would respond accordingly: the brightness of the sun would diminish, the winds would express a humane sigh, the clouds would weep, and the trees would shed their leaves, donning a veil of mourning even in the height of summer. It is worth noting that I seek to engage in a dialogue with the earth, pondering whether I am not, in part, composed of leaves and the very essence of the soil.
human: The indescribable innocence and beneficence of Nature, - of sun and wind and rain, of summer and winter, - such health, such cheer, they afford forever! and such sympathy have they ever with our race, that all Nature would be affected, and the sun’s brightness fade, and the winds would sigh humanely, and the clouds rain tears, and the woods shed their leaves and put on mourning in midsummer, if any man should ever for a just cause grieve. Shall I not have intelligence with the earth? Am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself?
base: Nature’s innocent and kind spirit, with the sun, wind, and rain, and the changing seasons of summer and winter, brings a lasting feeling of health and happiness. There is a deep bond between Nature and people so strong that if someone truly felt sad for a good reason, all of Nature would react: the sun would grow dimmer, the winds would sigh gently, the clouds would weep, and the trees would drop their leaves, wearing a veil of sorrow even in the middle of summer. I wonder if I, too, am made of leaves and the very heart of the earth, and if I am speaking to the ground in a way that matters.
finetuned: The indescribable innocence and goodness of Nature, the sun, the wind, the rain, summer, winter, give an eternal health and happiness. The sympathy between Nature and man is so deep that if any man were to feel true sorrow for just cause, all Nature would feel it, - the brightness of the sun would dim, the winds would sigh humanly, the clouds would weep, the trees would shed their leaves, and wear a veil of mourning, even in summer. I wish to converse with the earth, and wonder if I am not partly of leaves and the very heart of the soil.

title: Heart of Darkness
input:
The manager positioned himself beside the wheel, murmuring confidentially about the imperative of navigating well down the river before nightfall. It was at this moment that I observed a clearing in the distance along the riverside, accompanied by the outlines of what appeared to be a building. "What is this?" I inquired. He clapped his hands in amazement and exclaimed, "The station!" I immediately maneuvered the vessel closer while maintaining a cautious speed. 

Through my binoculars, I discerned the slope of a hill dotted with sparse trees, entirely devoid of undergrowth. A long, deteriorating structure atop the hill was partially obscured by tall grass; the expansive gaps in the peaked roof appeared dark from a distance. The surrounding jungle and woods formed a striking backdrop. There was an absence of any enclosure or fencing; however, it was evident that one had once existed, as I noted half a dozen slender posts remaining in a row near the house, each crudely trimmed and adorned with rounded carved balls at their upper ends. The rails or similar barriers that had previously connected them had vanished, enveloped by the encroaching forest. The riverbank remained clear, revealing a white man beneath a hat resembling a cart-wheel who was gesturing insistently with his entire arm. Upon scrutinizing the edges of the forest both above and below, I became increasingly convinced that I could perceive movements—human figures gliding discreetly to and fro. I proceeded past with caution, subsequently halting the engines to allow the vessel to drift downstream. The man on the shore began to call out, urging us to dock. "We have been attacked," the manager shouted in alarm. "I know—I know. It is all right," the other responded, his tone remarkably cheerful. "Come along. It is all right. I am glad."
human:
“The manager stood by the wheel murmuring confidentially about the necessity of getting well away down the river before dark at all events, when I saw in the distance a clearing on the riverside and the outlines of some sort of building. ‘What’s this?’ I asked. He clapped his hands in wonder. ‘The station!’ he cried. I edged in at once, still going half-speed.

“Through my glasses I saw the slope of a hill interspersed with rare trees and perfectly free from undergrowth. A long decaying building on the summit was half buried in the high grass; the large holes in the peaked roof gaped black from afar; the jungle and the woods made a background. There was no enclosure or fence of any kind; but there had been one apparently, for near the house half-a-dozen slim posts remained in a row, roughly trimmed, and with their upper ends ornamented with round carved balls. The rails, or whatever there had been between, had disappeared. Of course the forest surrounded all that. The river-bank was clear, and on the waterside I saw a white man under a hat like a cart-wheel beckoning persistently with his whole arm. Examining the edge of the forest above and below, I was almost certain I could see movements - human forms gliding here and there. I steamed past prudently, then stopped the engines and let her drift down. The man on the shore began to shout, urging us to land. ‘We have been attacked,’ screamed the manager. ‘I know - I know. It’s all right,’ yelled back the other, as cheerful as you please. ‘Come along. It’s all right. I am glad.’

"What is that?" I asked. He slapped his hands and said, "The station!" I moved the boat closer, going slow. With binoculars, I saw a hill with trees, no underbrush. A broken building on top of the hill was hidden by tall grass. The roof had big gaps, looking dark from far away. The jungle and woods around it were sharp against the background. There was no fence or enclosure, but I saw six posts in a line near the house, cut short and with rounded balls on top. The rails that once connected them were gone, swallowed by the forest. The riverbank was clear, showing a white man under a hat like a cart wheel, waving his arm. Looking around the forest edges, I saw people moving quietly. I kept going carefully, then stopped the engine so the boat could drift down. The man on land started shouting, telling us to come in. "We've been attacked," the manager cried. "I know—I know. It's all right," the other said, sounding happy. "Come on. It's all right. I'm glad."

title: Heart of Darkness
input: His presence seemed to embody a profound darkness. I regarded him as one might observe someone at the bottom of a ravine where light rarely penetrates. However, my time to attend to him was limited, as I was assisting the engine driver in disassembling the leaking cylinders, straightening a bent connecting rod, and managing other similar tasks. My environment was often chaotic, filled with rust, metal shavings, nuts, bolts, wrenches, hammers, and ratchet drills—items I typically found challenging to work with. I looked after the small forge we were fortunate to have on board and labored diligently amidst what felt like a disorganized pile of scrap, unless my condition prevented me from standing. Overall, my efforts were focused on maintaining the machinery while navigating the difficulties of my surroundings.
human: “His was an impenetrable darkness. I looked at him as you peer down at a man who is lying at the bottom of a precipice where the sun never shines. But I had not much time to give him, because I was helping the engine-driver to take to pieces the leaky cylinders, to straighten a bent connecting-rod, and in other such matters. I lived in an infernal mess of rust, filings, nuts, bolts, spanners, hammers, ratchet-drills - things I abominate, because I don’t get on with them. I tended the little forge we fortunately had aboard; I toiled wearily in a wretched scrap-heap - unless I had the shakes too bad to stand.

I was helping the engine driver take apart leaking cylinders, fix a bent rod, and do other things like that. The place was always loud and messy, full of rust, metal bits, nuts, bolts, wrenches, hammers, and drills. Those things usually made me uneasy. I kept the small forge we had on the ship and worked hard in what felt like a heap of scrap, unless I was too sick to stand. Most of the time, I was just trying to keep the machines running while dealing with the mess around me.

title: Heart of Darkness
input: In essence, during my childhood, I harbored a profound fascination for maps. I would spend countless hours studying regions such as South America, Africa, and Australia, immersing myself in the wonders of exploration. At that time, there existed numerous blank spaces on the globe, and whenever I encountered a particularly enticing area on a map—though, in truth, all of them appeared inviting—I would place my finger on it and declare, “When I grow up, I shall travel there.” The North Pole was among these alluring destinations that I distinctly recall. However, I have yet to visit it and do not intend to pursue that aspiration now, as the allure has diminished. Furthermore, various other locations were scattered across the hemispheres. I have had the opportunity to visit some of those places, and the experiences are best left unexamined. Nevertheless, there remained one destination—the largest and most uncharted, so to speak—that I longed to explore.
human: “Now when I was a little chap I had a passion for maps. I would look for hours at South America, or Africa, or Australia, and lose myself in all the glories of exploration. At that time there were many blank spaces on the earth, and when I saw one that looked particularly inviting on a map (but they all look that) I would put my finger on it and say, ‘When I grow up I will go there.’ The North Pole was one of these places, I remember. Well, I haven’t been there yet, and shall not try now. The glamour’s off. Other places were scattered about the hemispheres. I have been in some of them, and... well, we won’t talk about that. But there was one yet - the biggest, the most blank, so to speak - that I had a hankering after.

Back then, there were a lot of blank spots on the world map, and every time I saw a place that looked cool—well, actually, every place did—my finger would go there and I’d say, “One day, I’m going to travel there.” The North Pole was one of those places I remembered clearly. But I never went there and don’t plan to anymore, because it doesn’t feel as exciting now. There were other places all over the world I got to visit, and those experiences are best left alone. But there was still one place—the biggest and most unknown one—that I always wanted to see.

There were other places in the other hemispheres, which I have visited, and I have no desire to speak of them. There was still one place, - the biggest and the most unexplored, so to speak, - which I longed to go to.

title: Heart of Darkness
input: She extended her arms as if reaching for a departing figure, stretching them back with her pale hands clasped against the dimming light of the window. It may seem unlikely, but I could see him quite clearly at that moment. It seems that this poignant image will remain with me for as long as I live, and I may also remember her—a tragic and familiar presence—who, in this gesture, resembles another sorrowful figure adorned with powerless allure, reaching bare brown arms over the shimmering darkness of the stream. Then, in a soft voice, she remarked, "He died as he lived." This scene captures a blend of loss and remembrance.
human: “She put out her arms as if after a retreating figure, stretching them back and with clasped pale hands across the fading and narrow sheen of the window. Never see him! I saw him clearly enough then. I shall see this eloquent phantom as long as I live, and I shall see her, too, a tragic and familiar Shade, resembling in this gesture another one, tragic also, and bedecked with powerless charms, stretching bare brown arms over the glitter of the infernal stream, the stream of darkness. She said suddenly very low, ‘He died as he lived.’

I could see him clearly then, even though it might seem strange. That image will stay with me forever, along with her—a tragic, familiar figure—who looked like another sorrowful person, with arms that didn’t seem to have any power, reaching across the shimmering dark of the stream. She whispered, “He died as he lived.” The scene mixes loss and memory.

It is not improbable that I could see him distinctly then. This touching picture will live with me as long as I live, and I shall remember her - the tragic and familiar figure - who, in this gesture, is like another tragic figure, girdled with helpless seduction, with bare brown arms stretched over the glistening darkness of the stream. Then, in a low voice, she said, “He died as he lived.”

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: I consider my departure from Colonel Lloyd's plantation to be one of the most significant events in my life. It is possible, and indeed quite likely, that had I not been relocated from that plantation to Baltimore, I would today find myself, rather than seated at my own table experiencing freedom and the joys of home while composing this narrative, in the distressing confines of slavery. The move to Baltimore established the foundation and opened the door to all my future successes. I have consistently viewed this event as the initial clear indication of that kind providence which has continuously accompanied me and enriched my life with numerous blessings. Furthermore, I found the selection of myself to be rather remarkable. There were several other enslaved children who could have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore, including those who were younger, those who were older, and those who were of a similar age. Ultimately, I was chosen from among them all, being the first, last, and sole selection.

It is possible, and even quite probable, that but for the mere circumstance of being removed from that plantation to Baltimore, I should have to-day, instead of being here seated by my own table, in the enjoyment of freedom and the happiness of home, writing this Narrative, been confined in the galling chains of slavery. Going to live at Baltimore laid the foundation, and opened the gateway, to all my subsequent prosperity. I have ever regarded it as the first plain manifestation of that kind providence which has ever since attended me, and marked my life with so many favors. I regarded the selection of myself as being somewhat remarkable. There were a number of slave children that might have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore. There were those younger, those older, and those of the same age. I was chosen from among them all, and was the first, last, and only choice.

It's probably true that if I hadn't been sent from that place to Baltimore, I would still be in slavery, suffering in the dark, instead of sitting at my own table enjoying freedom and the happiness of home while writing this story. Moving to Baltimore was the start of everything else that came after. I've always seen this as the first sign that something good was happening to me, that God was watching over me and giving me many good things. Also, being chosen was special. There were other enslaved children who could have gone to Baltimore, some younger, some older, some the same age as me. But I was the one chosen, the first, the last, the only one.

There were several other slave children who could have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore, some younger, some older, and some of my own age. I was chosen from among them all, first, last, and sole choice.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: Colonel Lloyd's home plantation resembled a small country village, serving as the center for various mechanical operations for multiple farms. Tasks such as shoemaking, blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain grinding were all carried out by the enslaved individuals on this plantation. This environment had a distinctly business-like atmosphere, setting it apart from the neighboring farms. The plantation featured numerous houses, further enhancing its significance compared to others in the area. Known among the enslaved as the Great House Farm, being chosen to run errands there was highly valued by those on the outlying farms. This association with prestige elevated its status in their minds. A slave selected for errands at the Great House Farm felt a sense of pride comparable to a politician elected to the American Congress, as it represented the overseers' trust in them. This privilege was sought not only for the esteem it brought but also as an escape from the harsh conditions of fieldwork. The individual who received this honor frequently was regarded as the most capable and reliable, and competitors for this position worked hard to gain favor from their overseers, similar to how political candidates seek to win over the electorate. Such dynamics reveal parallels between the behavior of Colonel Lloyd's enslaved individuals and those involved in political life.
human: The home plantation of Colonel Lloyd wore the appearance of a country village. All the mechanical operations for all the farms were performed here. The shoemaking and mending, the blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain-grinding, were all performed by the slaves on the home plantation. The whole place wore a business-like aspect very unlike the neighboring farms. The number of houses, too, conspired to give it advantage over the neighboring farms. It was called by the slaves the Great House Farm. Few privileges were esteemed higher, by the slaves of the out-farms, than that of being selected to do errands at the Great House Farm. It was associated in their minds with greatness. A representative could not be prouder of his election to a seat in the American Congress, than a slave on one of the out-farms would be of his election to do errands at the Great House Farm. They regarded it as evidence of great confidence reposed in them by their overseers; and it was on this account, as well as a constant desire to be out of the field from under the driver’s lash, that they esteemed it a high privilege, one worth careful living for. He was called the smartest and most trusty fellow, who had this honor conferred upon him the most frequently. The competitors for this office sought as diligently to please their overseers, as the office-seekers in the political parties seek to please and deceive the people. The same traits of character might be seen in Colonel Lloyd’s slaves, as are seen in the slaves of the political parties.
base: Colonel Lloyd's home plantation looked like a small country village. It was the main place for many mechanical jobs on several farms. Enslaved people made shoes, fixed metal tools, built carts, made barrels, wove cloth, and ground grain there. The place had a business feel, different from the nearby farms. There were lots of houses, making it stand out. The enslaved called it the Great House Farm. Being sent there was a big deal. People on the other farms wanted to be chosen because it meant they were trusted. It felt like being elected to Congress. The honor was good for pride and a break from hard work. The person chosen was usually the best and most dependable. Others worked hard to be liked by the overseers, just like politicians try to win voters. This shows how the enslaved people's behavior was like that of people in politics.

Shoemaking, blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grinding grain, were all done by the slaves on this plantation. The air was business-like, and the place was more so than any other in the vicinity. There were many houses here, and the place was far more important than any other. It was known among the slaves as the Great House Farm, and to be chosen to run errands there was the highest honor among the slaves on the outlying farms. It was a slave’s highest honor to be chosen to run errands to the Great House Farm, and the feeling of pride was the same as in a slave who was chosen to be a member of the American Congress. It was not only to have the honor, but to have an opportunity to escape the toil of the fields. The slave who was chosen to run errands to the Great House Farm was thought to be the most capable and reliable, and the competitors for this honor worked hard to get the favor of the overseers, as political candidates work to get the favor of the people.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: I resided with Mr. Covey for a period of one year. During the initial six months of that year, there was scarcely a week in which he did not subject me to whipping. Additionally, I was seldom free from a sore back. Furthermore, my awkwardness was almost invariably the pretext for his inflicting punishment upon me. Moreover, we were worked fully to the point of endurance. In essence, long before daybreak we were up, our horses fed, and by the first approach of day we were off to the field with our hoes and ploughing teams. It is worth noting that Mr. Covey provided us with enough to eat, but scarcely enough time to eat it. Additionally, we were often less than five minutes in taking our meals. Furthermore, we were often in the field from the first approach of day until its last lingering ray had left us; and at saving-fodder time, midnight often caught us in the field binding blades.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: This mode of treatment exemplifies the broader system of deception and cruelty associated with slavery. It highlights how the approach taken seeks to instill a revulsion toward freedom by exposing the enslaved individuals only to its negative aspects. A notable example is when a slave, who has a fondness for molasses, steals some. In many instances, the master then goes to town and purchases a large quantity. Upon returning, the master forces the slave to consume the molasses until he becomes sickened by it. This method is similarly applied to discourage slaves from requesting more food than their standard allowance. When a slave exhausts his ration and seeks additional food, the master often reacts with anger but, rather than sending the slave away hungry, provides an excessive amount and mandates consumption within a specific timeframe. If the slave then expresses difficulty in eating the food, he may be punished for being discontented, as he is deemed neither satisfied nor fasting. This suggests a broader pattern of punitive measures aimed at controlling the desires and actions of enslaved individuals. The examples provided illustrate a prevalent practice within this system.
human: I have said that this mode of treatment is a part of the whole system of fraud and inhumanity of slavery. It is so. The mode here adopted to disgust the slave with freedom, by allowing him to see only the abuse of it, is carried out in other things. For instance, a slave loves molasses; he steals some. His master, in many cases, goes off to town, and buys a large quantity; he returns, takes his whip, and commands the slave to eat the molasses, until the poor fellow is made sick at the very mention of it. The same mode is sometimes adopted to make the slaves refrain from asking for more food than their regular allowance. A slave runs through his allowance, and applies for more. His master is enraged at him; but, not willing to send him off without food, gives him more than is necessary, and compels him to eat it within a given time. Then, if he complains that he cannot eat it, he is said to be satisfied neither full nor fasting, and is whipped for being hard to please! I have an abundance of such illustrations of the same principle, drawn from my own observation, but think the cases I have cited sufficient. The practice is a very common one.
base: This treatment shows the bigger picture of deception and cruelty in slavery. It shows how the method is meant to make people hate freedom by only showing them its bad sides. A good example is when a slave likes molasses and steals some. The master might go to town and buy a lot. Then the master makes the slave eat all of it until he feels sick. The same thing happens when a slave runs out of food and asks for more. The master gets angry but doesn’t send the slave away. Instead, he gives a lot more and tells them to eat quickly. If the slave says they can’t eat it, they get punished for being unhappy. They’re told they’re not satisfied or fasting. This shows how the system uses punishment to control what the slaves want and do. These examples show how common this practice was in the system.
finetuned: This treatment is the counterpart of the whole system of deception and cruelty connected with slavery. It is the attempt to create a disgust for freedom, by exhibiting the slaves only to its worst features. A slave who is fond of molasses, for instance, is sometimes caught stealing some. The master goes to town, buys a large quantity, and on returning, forces the slave to eat it until he is sick of it. In like manner the master sometimes tries to prevent the slaves from asking for more food than their ration. When a slave has finished his allowance, and asks for more, the master is angry, but instead of sending him away hungry, gives him a large quantity, and requires him to eat it in a given time. If the slave then says he can’t eat it, he is whipped for being discontented, because he is neither satisfied nor fasting.

title: A Study in Scarlet
input: The reader may consider me a hopeless busybody when I admit how much this man stimulated my curiosity and how often I tried to break through the reticence he showed concerning himself. Before passing judgment, however, one should remember how aimless my life was and how little there was to occupy my attention. My health prevented me from going out unless the weather was exceptionally mild, and I had no friends who would visit me and interrupt the monotony of my daily existence. Under these circumstances, I eagerly welcomed the small mystery surrounding my companion and spent much of my time attempting to unravel it.

title: A Study in Scarlet
input: Jefferson Hope suggested that it may be advisable to start immediately, speaking in a calm yet determined tone that indicated his awareness of the serious danger they faced. Overall, the plan seems feasible if they proceed cautiously.

Once on the road we are only two miles from the Ravine where the horses are waiting. By daybreak we should be half-way through the mountains.”

We can be halfway up the mountains by daybreak. It’s all very well, but we must be careful.”

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: With the stigma lifted, Hester experienced a profound release, as the burdens of shame and anguish lifted from her spirit. This highlights the significant relief she felt, which she had not fully recognized until she experienced the freedom. Following this impulse, she removed the formal cap that had restricted her hair, allowing it to cascade over her shoulders, rich and dark, creating a contrast of shadow and light that softened her features. A radiant and tender smile emerged around her mouth and shone in her eyes, suggesting a deep connection to her femininity. A vibrant blush returned to her cheeks, which had long been pale. The aspects of her identity, including her youth and beauty, returned from what is often perceived as an irreversible past, merging with her youthful hope and an unfamiliar happiness in this moment. This signifies that the heaviness of the earth and sky dissipated alongside their sorrow. Suddenly, as if illuminated by a divine presence, sunlight broke through, flooding the previously shadowed forest, brightening each green leaf, transforming the yellow fallen leaves into gold, and illuminating the gray trunks of the trees. Objects that once cast shadows now embodied brightness. The path of the little brook could be traced by its joyful sparkle as it wound its way into the heart of the woods, which had transformed into a place of joy.
human: The stigma gone, Hester heaved a long, deep sigh, in which the burden of shame and anguish departed from her spirit. O exquisite relief! She had not known the weight, until she felt the freedom! By another impulse, she took off the formal cap that confined her hair; and down it fell upon her shoulders, dark and rich, with at once a shadow and a light in its abundance, and imparting the charm of softness to her features. There played around her mouth, and beamed out of her eyes, a radiant and tender smile, that seemed gushing from the very heart of womanhood. A crimson flush was glowing on her cheek, that had been long so pale. Her sex, her youth, and the whole richness of her beauty, came back from what men call the irrevocable past, and clustered themselves, with her maiden hope, and a happiness before unknown, within the magic circle of this hour. And, as if the gloom of the earth and sky had been but the effluence of these two mortal hearts, it vanished with their sorrow. All at once, as with a sudden smile of heaven, forth burst the sunshine, pouring a very flood into the obscure forest, gladdening each green leaf, transmuting the yellow fallen ones to gold, and gleaming adown the gray trunks of the solemn trees. The objects that had made a shadow hitherto, embodied the brightness now. The course of the little brook might be traced by its merry gleam afar into the wood’s heart of mystery, which had become a mystery of joy.

She took off the cap that had kept her hair bound. Her hair fell over her shoulders, dark and thick. The contrast of shadow and light softened her face. A gentle smile came to her lips and stayed in her eyes. It showed she was connected to her femininity. A warm color returned to her cheeks, which had been pale for a long time. Parts of her identity—her youth, her beauty—came back from what people thought was lost. They mixed with her hope and a new kind of happiness. The heavy feeling of the earth and sky faded along with their sorrow. Then, as if touched by a divine light, the sun broke through. It filled the dark forest with brightness. Every green leaf shimmered. The yellow leaves turned gold. The gray trees glowed. Things that had cast shadows now had light. The little brook’s path could be seen by the way it sparkled as it moved through the woods, now a place of joy.

A sweet and tender smile was about her mouth, and in her eyes; a bright and tender blush returned to her cheeks, which had been long pale. The young and beautiful, which had been banished from her for ever, were now returned, and merged themselves in her youthful hope, and in a strange happiness of this hour. The weight of the earth and sky seemed to fall off together with their sorrow. All at once, as if from the presence of some angel, the sun broke through, and flooded the shadowed forest, and made every green leaf bright, and turned the yellow fallen leaves to gold, and lighted up the gray trunks of the trees. Objects that had been shadowy became bright; the path of the little brook might be followed by its sparkling mirth as it wound its way into the heart of the woods, which had become a joyous place.

title: The Scarlet Letter
input:
At times, a light flickered in the physician’s eyes, a burning blue that seemed foreboding, reminiscent of a furnace's glow. It was akin to the eerie flashes of fire that emerged from Bunyan’s terrifying doorway in the hillside, shimmering briefly on the face of the pilgrim. The ground where this dark miner was laboring may have revealed signs that fueled his determination. 

“This man,” he thought during one of these moments, “as pure as he appears, as spiritual as he seems, has inherited a potent animal nature from his parents. I will explore further in this direction.”

The soil where this dark miner was working had perchance shown indications that encouraged him.

“This man,” said he, at one such moment, to himself, “pure as they deem him, - all spiritual as he seems, - hath inherited a strong animal nature from his father or his mother. Let us dig a little further in the direction of this vein!”

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: What sets the physician's ecstasy apart from that of Satan is the presence of wonder within it. Following the recent incident, the interactions between the clergyman and the physician transformed in nature, although they appeared outwardly unchanged. Roger Chillingworth's intellect now had a clear direction, though it was not the path he had originally envisioned. While he maintained a calm, gentle demeanor, a quiet malice that had previously been hidden became active in this unfortunate old man. This suggests that he envisioned a form of revenge that was more intimate than any typically enacted by a mortal upon an enemy. He sought to become the trusted confidant to whom all fear, remorse, agony, and futile repentance could be revealed, along with the return of sinful thoughts that had been suppressed in vain. Ultimately, this hidden sorrow, which would have been met with compassion and forgiveness by the world, was intended to be laid bare before him, a figure characterized by a lack of empathy and forgiveness. This dark assortment of emotions would serve as a means to repay the debt of vengeance to the very individual who had wronged him.
human:
But what distinguished the physician’s ecstasy from Satan’s was the trait of wonder in it!

After the incident last described, the intercourse between the clergyman and the physician, though externally the same, was really of another character than it had previously been. The intellect of Roger Chillingworth had now a sufficiently plain path before it. It was not, indeed, precisely that which he had laid out for himself to tread. Calm, gentle, passionless, as he appeared, there was yet, we fear, a quiet depth of malice, hitherto latent, but active now, in this unfortunate old man, which led him to imagine a more intimate revenge than any mortal had ever wreaked upon an enemy. To make himself the one trusted friend, to whom should be confided all the fear, the remorse, the agony, the ineffectual repentance, the backward rush of sinful thoughts, expelled in vain! All that guilty sorrow, hidden from the world, whose great heart would have pitied and forgiven, to be revealed to him, the Pitiless, to him, the Unforgiving! All that dark treasure to be lavished on the very man, to whom nothing else could so adequately pay the debt of vengeance!

After the recent event, the way the clergyman and the physician spoke to each other changed, though it looked the same on the outside. Roger Chillingworth's mind now had a clear purpose, though it wasn't the one he first thought of. He stayed calm and gentle, but a quiet hate that had been hidden before came out in this unlucky old man. This shows he wanted a kind of revenge that was more personal than what most people would do to an enemy. He aimed to be the one people trusted most, the one who would hear all their fears, regrets, pain, and false repentances, along with the sinful thoughts they had tried to keep away. In the end, this hidden sadness, which the world would have understood and forgave, was meant to be shown to him, a man who didn't care much for compassion or forgiveness. This dark mix of feelings would be his way of getting back at the person who had hurt him.

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: The mariner informed Hester that he needed to arrange for an additional sleeping quarter beyond what had been agreed upon. He reassured her that there was no need for concern about scurvy or ship-related illnesses during the journey, as the presence of both a ship's surgeon and another doctor would mitigate health risks. He noted that the primary concern would be related to medications, especially since there was a significant supply of apothecary goods on board, which he had obtained through trade with a Spanish ship. Hester, taken aback by this news, asked for clarification, particularly regarding the possibility of an additional passenger.

“So, mistress,” said the mariner, “I must bid the steward make ready one more berth than you bargained for! No fear of scurvy or ship-fever, this voyage! What with the ship’s surgeon and this other doctor, our only danger will be from drug or pill; more by token, as there is a lot of apothecary’s stuff aboard, which I traded for with a Spanish vessel.”

“What mean you?” inquired Hester, startled more than she permitted to appear. “Have you another passenger?”

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: On this particular day, there may have been an expression that had never been observed before or, indeed, one that was not easily recognizable now; unless perhaps there existed an extraordinarily perceptive observer who could first understand her heart and then look for a related change in her face and demeanor. Such a sensitive soul might have believed that after enduring the scrutinizing gaze of the crowd for seven long years—viewed as a necessity, a punishment, and something akin to a harsh faith—she now willingly faced it one last time, aiming to transform her prolonged suffering into a sense of triumph. She might have quietly addressed the onlookers, saying, “Take a good look at the scarlet letter and its bearer! Soon, she will be out of your reach! In just a few hours, the profound and mysterious ocean will extinguish and conceal forever the mark you have forced upon her.” It may not be too far-fetched to imagine that Hester felt a twinge of regret as she was on the verge of gaining her freedom from a pain that had become entwined with her very existence. Could she not have experienced an overwhelming urge to savor one final, intense taste of the bitter experiences that had flavored most of her adult life? The future may hold for her a life that is rich, delightful, and invigorating, served in a beautiful golden cup; otherwise, it might leave her with an unavoidable weariness following the bitterness that had long been her companion.

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: He looked darkly at the clergyman and said that even if he had searched the whole earth, there was no place so secret, no high place or lowly place, where he could have escaped him, except on this very scaffold. Yet he trembled and turned to Hester with an expression of doubt and anxiety in his eyes. This was all the more evident because a feeble smile remained on his lips. Partly supported by Hester Prynne and holding one hand of little Pearl, the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale turned to the dignified and venerable rulers, to the holy ministers who were his brethren, and to the people, whose great heart was thoroughly appalled yet overflowing with tearful sympathy. They knew that some deep life-matter, which if full of sin was full of anguish and repentance likewise, was now to be laid open to them. The sun, but little past its meridian, shone down upon the clergyman and gave a distinctness to his figure as he stood out from all the earth to put in his plea of guilty at the bar of Eternal Justice.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: When a Sperm Whale is captured in the Southern Fishery, it is generally not customary to begin the process of cutting it up immediately, especially late at night. This task is extremely labor-intensive, does not conclude quickly, and requires the full attention of the crew. Consequently, the typical practice is to take in all sail and secure the helm, allowing the crew to rest in their hammocks until dawn. However, two crew members must remain on deck in rotation for an hour at a time to monitor the situation, ensuring that everything proceeds smoothly until morning.
human: When in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale, after long and weary toil, is brought alongside late at night, it is not, as a general thing at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; is not very soon completed; and requires all hands to set about it. Therefore, the common usage is to take in all sail; lash the helm a’lee; and then send every one below to his hammock till daylight, with the reservation that, until that time, anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, two and two for an hour, each couple, the crew in rotation shall mount the deck to see that all goes well.
base: When a sperm whale is caught in the southern fishery, they don’t start cutting it right away, especially at night. It’s a lot of work, takes a long time, and needs everyone’s focus. So they take in all the sails and secure the wheel, letting the crew rest in their hammocks until dawn. But two people have to stay on deck, taking turns every hour, to keep an eye on things and make sure everything goes smoothly until morning.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: Meanwhile, while supervising another section of the vessel, Captain Peleg vociferously expressed his frustrations from the stern in an alarming manner. I nearly believed he might cause the ship to capsize prior to the retrieval of the anchor; consequently, I found myself pausing with my handspike and instructed Queequeg to do likewise, reflecting on the dangers we both faced in embarking on our journey under the command of such a volatile pilot. Despite this, I reassured myself with the notion that there might be some hope in the pious Bildad, notwithstanding his seven hundred seventy-seventh sermon. However, my thoughts were abruptly interrupted by a sudden and sharp impact to my rear, and upon turning, I was appalled to discover Captain Peleg in the process of retracting his leg from my immediate vicinity. That experience marked my first encounter with physical reprimand.

I almost thought he would sink the ship before the anchor could be got up; involuntarily I paused on my handspike, and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the perils we both ran, in starting on the voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself, however, with the thought that in pious Bildad might be found some salvation, spite of his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay; when I felt a sudden sharp poke in my rear, and turning round, was horrified at the apparition of Captain Peleg in the act of withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: As evening approached, I felt reasonably certain that all of his activities and rituals had concluded, so I decided to check on him in his room. I knocked gently on the door, but received no response. Attempting to open it, I found it securely fastened from within. "Queequeg," I called softly through the keyhole, but there was only silence. "I say, Queequeg! Why don’t you respond? It’s me—Ishmael." Yet, the stillness persisted, which began to concern me. I had given him ample time, and it crossed my mind that he may have experienced a medical issue. Peering through the keyhole, I was met with an odd angle, which provided a rather limited view. I could see only part of the bed frame and a section of the wall, with no further insight. It caught my attention to see Queequeg’s harpoon resting against the wall. The landlady had taken it from him the previous evening before we went to our room. This struck me as unusual, yet since the harpoon was indeed there and he rarely ventured out without it, it seemed likely he was still inside.

I tried to open it, but it was fastened inside. “Queequeg,” said I softly through the key-hole: - all silent. “I say, Queequeg! why don’t you speak? It’s I - Ishmael.” But all remained still as before. I began to grow alarmed. I had allowed him such abundant time; I thought he might have had an apoplectic fit. I looked through the key-hole; but the door opening into an odd corner of the room, the key-hole prospect was but a crooked and sinister one. I could only see part of the foot-board of the bed and a line of the wall, but nothing more. I was surprised to behold resting against the wall the wooden shaft of Queequeg’s harpoon, which the landlady the evening previous had taken from him, before our mounting to the chamber. That’s strange, thought I; but at any rate, since the harpoon stands yonder, and he seldom or never goes abroad without it, therefore he must be inside here, and no possible mistake.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: In essence, one must consider how, within this designated quest, Ahab fails to make contact with any land. Does his crew subsist solely on air? Surely, he must pause for water. However, this is not the case. For an extended period, the sun, akin to a circus performer, has traversed its fiery path, requiring no sustenance other than that which resides within itself. Thus, Ahab. Furthermore, it is important to observe the nature of the whaler. While other vessels are burdened with foreign goods destined for distant docks, the wandering whale ship carries only herself, her crew, their weapons, and their necessities. She contains the equivalent of an entire lake within her spacious hold. She is balanced with useful provisions rather than merely with unusable materials such as pig lead and kentledge. She retains years' worth of water. This water, sourced from the pristine wells of Nantucket, is preferred by the Nantucketer in the Pacific after three years at sea, over the brackish fluid acquired just the day before from the rivers of Peru or India. Thus, while other ships may have traveled from New York to China and back, stopping at numerous ports, the whale ship may not have encountered even a single grain of soil during that time; her crew having seen no one other than fellow sailors adrift like themselves. Consequently, if one were to inform them that another flood had occurred, they would merely respond, "Well, boys, here is the ark!"

For a long time, now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring, and needs no sustenance but what’s in himself. So Ahab. Mark this, too, in the whaler. While other hulls are loaded down with alien stuff, to be transferred to foreign wharves; the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake’s contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with utilities; not altogether with unusable pig-lead and kentledge. She carries years’ water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water; which, when three years afloat, the Nantucketer, in the Pacific, prefers to drink before the brackish fluid, but yesterday rafted off in casks, from the Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is, that, while other ships may have gone to China from New York, and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship, in all that interval, may not have sighted one grain of soil; her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that did you carry them the news that another flood had come; they would only answer - “Well, boys, here’s the ark!”

This one carries only itself, the crew, their weapons, and what they need. She holds as much water as a whole lake. She’s filled with useful things, not useless stuff like lead and kentledge. title: Black Beauty
input: This situation could not continue indefinitely; it seems unlikely that any horse could maintain its footing under such conditions, as the pain might be too significant. I tripped and fell rather hard on my knees. Smith was thrown off due to my fall, and given the speed at which I was moving, it is possible he landed quite forcefully. I managed to regain my feet and limped over to the edge of the road, where the ground was free of stones. The moon had just risen above the hedge, and in its light, I could see Smith lying a few yards away from me. He did not get up; he made a small attempt to do so but then let out a deep groan. I could have groaned as well, for I was experiencing considerable pain in both my foot and knees; however, horses tend to endure their discomfort quietly. I remained silent, standing still and listening. I heard another heavy groan from Smith; although he lay fully illuminated by the moon, I could not see any movement from him. Feeling helpless for both him and myself, I listened intently for the sound of a horse, wheels, or footsteps. The road was not heavily traveled, and at this hour, we might wait for quite some time before assistance arrived. I stood there, observing and listening. The night was calm and pleasant, with only the soft notes of a nightingale breaking the silence, and the only movement was from the white clouds near the moon and a brown owl that glided over the hedge. This scene reminded me of summer nights long ago, when I would lie beside my mother in the lovely green meadow at Farmer Grey's.

Smith was flung off by my fall, and, owing to the speed I was going at, he must have fallen with great force. I soon recovered my feet and limped to the side of the road, where it was free from stones. The moon had just risen above the hedge, and by its light I could see Smith lying a few yards beyond me. He did not rise; he made one slight effort to do so, and then there was a heavy groan. I could have groaned, too, for I was suffering intense pain both from my foot and knees; but horses are used to bear their pain in silence. I uttered no sound, but I stood there and listened. One more heavy groan from Smith; but though he now lay in the full moonlight I could see no motion. I could do nothing for him nor myself, but, oh! how I listened for the sound of horse, or wheels, or footsteps! The road was not much frequented, and at this time of the night we might stay for hours before help came to us. I stood watching and listening. It was a calm, sweet April night; there were no sounds but a few low notes of a nightingale, and nothing moved but the white clouds near the moon and a brown owl that flitted over the hedge. It made me think of the summer nights long ago, when I used to lie beside my mother in the green pleasant meadow at Farmer Grey's.

title: Black Beauty
input: Two days following the accident, Blantyre came to see me. He patted me and offered extensive praise. He informed Lord George that he believed the horse was aware of Annie's peril, just as he was. He stated, “I could not have controlled him even if I had wanted to; she should never ride another horse.” Through their discussion, I learned that my young mistress was now safe and would soon be able to ride again. This news brought me joy, and I began to anticipate a happy future.

title: Black Beauty
input: Lady Harriet, who stayed at the hall, was often unwell and did not go out in the carriage. Lady Anne, on the other hand, tended to enjoy horseback riding with her brother or cousins. She was quite skilled at riding and was known to be cheerful and gentle, in addition to her beauty. She chose me as her horse and affectionately named me "Black Auster." I found these rides to be quite enjoyable, especially in the crisp, fresh air, sometimes accompanied by Ginger and at other times by Lizzie. Lizzie was a lively bay mare, almost thoroughbred, and was quite popular among the gentlemen due to her graceful movements and spirited nature. However, Ginger, who was more familiar with Lizzie, suggested that she could be somewhat anxious. Overall, these experiences tended to create a pleasant atmosphere for our rides.

title: Black Beauty
input: Jerry maintained an exceptionally clean environment for us and provided as much variety in our diet as he could, ensuring that we received an ample quantity of food. Furthermore, he consistently supplied us with an adequate amount of clean, fresh water, which he allowed to remain accessible to us both day and night, with the exception of moments when we returned from our labor in a warm state. It is worth noting that some individuals believe that a horse should not have unrestricted access to water; however, I have observed that when we are permitted to drink according to our needs, we tend to consume only small amounts at a time. This approach benefits us significantly more than consuming large quantities all at once, which typically occurs when we are deprived of water until we become thirsty and uncomfortable. Additionally, some grooms would return home to enjoy their beer, leaving us with nothing but dry hay and oats for hours, without any moisture to accompany them. Consequently, we would inevitably consume excessive amounts of water in a single instance, which could negatively affect our respiratory health and sometimes lead to stomach discomfort. In essence, one of the most valuable aspects of our time here was the respite we received on Sundays. We exerted considerable effort throughout the week, and I sincerely believe that we would have struggled to maintain our stamina without that day of rest. Moreover, it provided us with the opportunity to enjoy each other's company, during which time I learned about the history of my companion.

Some people say that a horse ought not to drink all he likes; but I know if we are allowed to drink when we want it we drink only a little at a time, and it does us a great deal more good than swallowing down half a bucketful at a time, because we have been left without till we are thirsty and miserable. Some grooms will go home to their beer and leave us for hours with our dry hay and oats and nothing to moisten them; then of course we gulp down too much at once, which helps to spoil our breathing and sometimes chills our stomachs. But the best thing we had here was our Sundays for rest; we worked so hard in the week that I do not think we could have kept up to it but for that day; besides, we had then time to enjoy each other's company. It was on these days that I learned my companion's history.

title: The Good Soldier
input: She had not spoken to Edward in many years; their conversations were limited to logistical matters such as train schedules and hiring staff. That afternoon, however, she felt compelled to confront him. He was precisely as she remembered. It was akin to reopening a book after ten years, only to find the text unchanged. His motives remained the same. He had refrained from discussing the case because he did not want her to tarnish her thoughts with the notion that a brother officer could engage in blackmail. He sought to protect the reputation of his former love. However, it was clear that she was not concerned for her husband. He insisted repeatedly that there was nothing else in the world that could be held against him. She did not believe his assurances.

title: The Good Soldier
input: This represents the saddest narrative I have ever encountered. My wife and I had been acquainted with the Ashburnhams for nine seasons in the town of Nauheim, cultivating a connection that was both intimate and characterized by a relaxed familiarity, akin to the relationship between a well-fitted glove and one’s hand. We were familiar with Captain and Mrs. Ashburnham to the extent that one could be acquainted with another individual; however, in a deeper sense, we were unaware of their true selves. It is worth noting that such a situation appears to be uniquely characteristic of English individuals. Until today, when I take the time to contemplate my understanding of this tragic situation, I must acknowledge that I knew virtually nothing about them. Moreover, six months prior, I had never visited England, and I certainly had not delved into the complexities of the English heart; my experiences had only skimmed the surface.
human: THIS is the saddest story I have ever heard. We had known the Ashburnhams for nine seasons of the town of Nauheim with an extreme intimacy - or, rather with an acquaintanceship as loose and easy and yet as close as a good glove's with your hand. My wife and I knew Captain and Mrs Ashburnham as well as it was possible to know anybody, and yet, in another sense, we knew nothing at all about them. This is, I believe, a state of things only possible with English people of whom, till today, when I sit down to puzzle out what I know of this sad affair, I knew nothing whatever. Six months ago I had never been to England, and, certainly, I had never sounded the depths of an English heart. I had known the shallows.

Even now, when I think about how little I knew about their tragedy, I realize I knew almost nothing. Six months before, I hadn’t even been to England, and I hadn’t really understood the English heart—just touched the surface.

Until to-day, when I am thinking of my knowledge of this sad business, I must confess that I knew very little of them. And six months before that I had never been in England, and I had never touched the English heart - I had only touched its skin.

Mr. O’Connor had been hired by Tierney’s agent to campaign in one section of the ward. However, due to the unpleasant weather and his leaky boots, he spent much of the day by the fire in the Committee Room on Wicklow Street, accompanied by Jack, the elderly caretaker. They had been sitting there since darkness had fallen on the short October day. It was the sixth of October, and the outdoors was dreary and cold.

Mr. O’Connor tore a strip from the card and lit it to ignite his cigarette. As he did this, the flame illuminated a leaf of dark, glossy ivy tucked into the lapel of his coat. The old man observed him closely and then picked up the cardboard again, beginning to fan the fire gently while his companion smoked.

title: Leviathan
input: From this we may infer that when we believe any statement to be true, not because of the thing itself or because of principles of natural reason, but because of the authority and good opinion we have of the person who said it, then the speaker, or the person we believe in and trust, and whose word we accept, is the object of our faith, and the honor done in believing is done to that person alone. Consequently, when we believe that the Scriptures are the word of God, without having any immediate revelation from God himself, our belief, faith, and trust is in the Church, whose word we accept and rest upon. And those who believe what a prophet relates to them in the name of God accept the word of the prophet, do honor to him, and trust and believe in him regarding the truth of what he relates, whether he is a true prophet or a false one. And so it is also with all other history. For if I should not believe all that is written by historians about the glorious acts of Alexander or Caesar, I do not think the ghost of Alexander or Caesar would have any just cause to be offended, or anyone else except the historian. If Livy says the gods once made a cow speak, and we do not believe it, we do not distrust God in that, but Livy. So it is evident that whatever we believe on no other reason than what is drawn from the authority of men alone and their writings, whether they are sent from God or not, is faith in men only.

title: Leviathan
input: This highlights that even when individuals are willing to adhere to laws, disputes regarding a person's actions can still arise. These disputes can be categorized into two main questions: first, whether an action was taken or not; and second, if an action was taken, whether it was in accordance with the law or not. The first type is referred to as a question of fact, while the second is identified as a question of right. Consequently, unless the parties involved agree to accept the decision of a third party, known as an arbitrator, they remain in a state of conflict. Ultimately, it is a principle of natural law that those in dispute should submit their rights to the judgment of an arbitrator.
human: And because, though men be never so willing to observe these Lawes, there may neverthelesse arise questions concerning a mans action; First, whether it were done, or not done; Secondly (if done) whether against the Law, or not against the Law; the former whereof, is called a question Of Fact; the later a question Of Right; therefore unlesse the parties to the question, Covenant mutually to stand to the sentence of another, they are as farre from Peace as ever. This other, to whose Sentence they submit, is called an ARBITRATOR. And therefore it is of the Law of Nature, "That they that are at controversie, submit their Right to the judgement of an Arbitrator."
base: This shows that even when people follow the law, disagreements about what someone did can still happen. There are two main types of questions. One is whether the person actually did something. The other is whether what they did was allowed by the law. The first is a question of fact. The second is a question of right. Unless the people involved agree to let someone else, called an arbitrator, decide, they stay in conflict. Naturally, the idea is that those who are arguing should let an arbitrator decide their rights.
finetuned: And it is here that we find that even when men are willing to be bound by law, there are yet disputes about what a man has done; and these disputes are of two kinds. One is, whether an action was taken, or not; and the other is, if an action was taken, whether it was done lawfully, or not. The former is called a question of fact; the latter, a question of right. And unless the parties agree to leave the decision of either to the judgment of a third person, called an arbitrator, they are still in a state of conflict; and it is a principle of natural law that the parties in conflict shall submit their right to the judgment of an arbitrator.

title: Leviathan
input: When they are considered as his own, he is then called a natural person; and when they are considered as representing the words and actions of another, he is then a feigned or artificial person. It is worth noting that the word person is Latin; instead of it the Greeks have prosopon, which signifies the face, as persona in Latin signifies the disguise or outward appearance of a man, counterfeited on the stage, and sometimes more particularly that part of it which disguises the face, as a mask or visor. Furthermore, from the stage it has been transferred to any representer of speech and action, as well in tribunals as in theaters. In essence, a person is the same as an actor, both on the stage and in common conversation; and to personate is to act or represent oneself or another; and he who acts another is said to bear his person or act in his name (in which sense Cicero uses it when he says, "Unus Sustineo Tres Personas; Mei, Adversarii, & Judicis, I bear three persons: my own, my adversary's, and the judge's"), and is called on diverse occasions diversely, as a representer or representative, a lieutenant, a vicar, an attorney, a deputy, a procurator, an actor, and the like.
