title: Leviathan
input: When the representative is a single individual, if he borrows money or incurs a debt through a contract, he alone bears responsibility; the other members do not share this liability. If the entity of the political body is embodied in one person who borrows money from an outsider—specifically, an individual who is not part of the same body—then the debt is solely that of the representative. This is because, should he possess authority through formal documentation to compel the members to repay what he has borrowed, he would consequently hold sovereignty over them. Therefore, such a grant would be void, as it stems from an error typically associated with human nature, and is an insufficient indication of the grantor's intent. Conversely, if the authority is acknowledged, the representative becomes sovereign, thereby falling outside the current discussion, which pertains solely to subordinate bodies. Consequently, no member is obligated to repay the borrowed debt; the responsibility rests solely with the representative. The lender, being an outsider to the formal documentation and the qualifications of the body, recognizes only those individuals who are engaged as debtors. Since the representative is capable of binding himself alone, he is the only debtor in this instance, and he must therefore repay the lender either from the common fund, if available, or from his own personal assets.
human: When The Representative Is One Man, If He Borrow Mony, Or Owe It, By Contract; He Is Lyable Onely, The Members Not If the person of the Body Politique being in one man, borrow mony of a stranger, that is, of one that is not of the same Body, (for no Letters need limit borrowing, seeing it is left to mens own inclinations to limit lending) the debt is the Representatives. For if he should have Authority from his Letters, to make the members pay what he borroweth, he should have by consequence the Soveraignty of them; and therefore the grant were either voyd, as proceeding from Errour, commonly incident to humane Nature, and an unsufficient signe of the will of the Granter; or if it be avowed by him, then is the Representer Soveraign, and falleth not under the present question, which is onely of Bodies subordinate. No member therefore is obliged to pay the debt so borrowed, but the Representative himselfe: because he that lendeth it, being a stranger to the Letters, and to the qualification of the Body, understandeth those onely for his debtors, that are engaged; and seeing the Representer can ingage himselfe, and none else, has him onely for Debtor; who must therefore pay him, out of the common stock (if there be any), or (if there be none) out of his own estate.
base: When a representative is a single person, if he borrows money or takes on a debt through a contract, he is the only one responsible. The others aren’t liable. If the political body is represented by one person who borrows from someone outside the body, the debt is just his. Why? Because if he had the power to make the others pay, he’d be in charge. That wouldn’t work. So the grant of power is wrong, a mistake people often make. It doesn’t show the right intent. But if the power is real, the representative is in charge, and this isn’t about them. So no one else has to pay. The debt is on the representative. The lender doesn’t know the body’s rules. He only sees the person who borrowed. Since the representative can take on the debt alone, he’s the only one who needs to pay. He can use the group’s money if it’s there, or his own.
finetuned: When the representative is a single man, if he borrows money or incurs a debt by contract, he alone is liable, and the rest are not. If the body politic is vested in one man, who borrows money from an alien, that is, from a man not belonging to the same body, the debt is only his. For, if he hath authority by writing to exact from the members the payment of what he hath borrowed, he hath sovereignty over them, and such a grant is void, because it is the error of a man's nature, and a very poor evidence of his intention. But if the authority is allowed, the representative is sovereign, and is out of the question; the subject of this discourse being only inferior bodies. And therefore no member is liable to the payment of the borrowed debt; it is only on the part of the representative; and he must pay it to the lender, either out of the common stock, if there be any, or out of his own estate.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: If a guinea is the weekly pension of an individual, that person can use it to purchase a specific amount of necessities, comforts, and entertainment throughout the week. The extent of these purchases reflects the individual's actual wealth and their true weekly income. This income does not equate to both the guinea and the items it can buy; rather, it aligns more closely with one of these values. It is more accurate to consider the value of the goods purchased rather than the mere presence of the guinea itself.
human: Thus, if a guinea be the weekly pension of a particular person, he can in the course of the week purchase with it a certain quantity of subsistence, conveniencies, and amusements. In proportion as this quantity is great or small, so are his real riches, his real weekly revenue. His weekly revenue is certainly not equal both to the guinea and to what can be purchased with it, but only to one or other of those two equal values, and to the latter more properly than to the former, to the guinea’s worth rather than to the guinea.
base: A guinea is the weekly pension given to an individual. With that amount, the person can buy a certain amount of food, comfort, and entertainment for the week. How much they can spend shows their real wealth and how much they actually earn each week. The money isn't the same as both the guinea and the things it can buy. It's more like the value of what they actually buy. It's better to look at the value of the goods they purchase than just the fact that they have the guinea.
finetuned: If a guinea is the weekly pension of any man, he will use it to buy a certain quantity of necessaries, comforts, and amusements for the week; and the quantity of these, which he buys, is an exact measure of his real wealth and his real weekly revenue. It is not the guinea, and the goods which it will buy, that constitute this revenue; it is the guinea itself, or the goods which it will buy, whichever of the two may be the true measure of it. It is the value of the goods, and not the mere existence of the guinea, that constitutes the revenue.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: It is worth noting that there exist two scenarios in which it is generally beneficial to impose certain burdens on foreign goods to promote domestic industry. Additionally, there are two further situations in which it may warrant careful consideration: the first pertains to the extent to which it is appropriate to maintain the unrestricted importation of specific foreign goods, while the second concerns the degree and manner in which it may be suitable to reinstate such unrestricted importation after it has been temporarily suspended.
human: As there are two cases in which it will generally be advantageous to lay some burden upon foreign for the encouragement of domestic industry, so there are two others in which it may sometimes be a matter of deliberation, in the one, how far it is proper to continue the free importation of certain foreign goods; and, in the other, how far, or in what manner, it may be proper to restore that free importation, after it has been for some time interrupted.
base: There are two cases where putting extra costs on foreign products helps support local businesses. Then there are two more situations that need thought: one is whether it's right to keep bringing in certain foreign goods without limits, and the other is how and how much to bring them back once they've been stopped temporarily.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input:
North America, while not as wealthy as England, is experiencing significant growth and advancing more rapidly towards greater wealth. A key indicator of a country's prosperity is its population growth. In Great Britain and many European nations, populations are not expected to double in less than five hundred years. In contrast, populations in the British colonies in North America have been observed to double in about twenty to twenty-five years. This increase in population is not primarily due to continuous immigration but rather to a high birth rate. It is reported that those who live into old age often see several dozen descendants. 

In North America, the rewards for labor are substantial, turning large families into sources of wealth rather than burdens for parents. Each child's labor is estimated to provide a significant financial benefit before they leave home. Additionally, a young widow with several children may be viewed positively in terms of potential marriage prospects, which is not the case in Europe where such women have limited opportunities. The value placed on children serves as a strong incentive for marriage, leading to a trend of early marriages among the population. Despite the rapid population growth resulting from these early unions, there remains a persistent complaint regarding the shortage of available labor. The demand for workers and the resources allocated for their support appear to be increasing more quickly than the supply of laborers.
human: But though North America is not yet so rich as England, it is much more thriving, and advancing with much greater rapidity to the further acquisition of riches. The most decisive mark of the prosperity of any country is the increase of the number of its inhabitants. In Great Britain, and most other European countries, they are not supposed to double in less than five hundred years. In the British colonies in North America, it has been found that they double in twenty or five-and-twenty years. Nor in the present times is this increase principally owing to the continual importation of new inhabitants, but to the great multiplication of the species. Those who live to old age, it is said, frequently see there from fifty to a hundred, and sometimes many more, descendants from their own body. Labour is there so well rewarded, that a numerous family of children, instead of being a burden, is a source of opulence and prosperity to the parents. The labour of each child, before it can leave their house, is computed to be worth a hundred pounds clear gain to them. A young widow with four or five young children, who, among the middling or inferior ranks of people in Europe, would have so little chance for a second husband, is there frequently courted as a sort of fortune. The value of children is the greatest of all encouragements to marriage. We cannot, therefore, wonder that the people in North America should generally marry very young. Notwithstanding the great increase occasioned by such early marriages, there is a continual complaint of the scarcity of hands in North America. The demand for labourers, the funds destined for maintaining them increase, it seems, still faster than they can find labourers to employ.

North America isn’t as rich as England, but it’s growing fast and getting richer quicker. A sign of a country’s luck is how fast its people grow. In Britain and Europe, populations don’t double in less than five hundred years. But in North America, colonies there, populations double in twenty to twenty-five years. That growth isn’t from lots of new people coming in, but from lots of babies being born. People who live a long time often have dozens of kids.

In North America, working hard pays off. Big families are a source of money, not a problem for parents. Each child helps pay for their own living before they leave home. A young woman with kids might be seen as a good match, unlike in Europe where such women have fewer chances. Valuing kids pushes people to marry early. Even with all that growth, there’s still a problem: not enough workers. Jobs and money for workers are growing faster than the number of people ready to work.

Each child's labour is worth a good deal of money before it goes from home. And a young widow with several children is thought to have a good prospect of marrying, which is not the case in Europe, where such women have few chances of marriage. The value of children is a strong motive to marriage, and this produces an early marriage among the whole body of the people. The great increase of the population which arises from these early unions, is yet accompanied by a continual complaint of the want of labour. The demand of workers and of the provision for them is increasing more rapidly than the supply of labourers.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: The price of the coarse metals, and still more that of the precious metals, at the most fertile mines in the world must necessarily more or less affect their price at every other mine. The price of copper in Japan must have some influence on its price at the copper mines in Europe. The price of silver in Peru, or the quantity of labour or of other goods it will purchase there, must have some influence on its price not only at the silver mines of Europe but also at those of China. After the discovery of the mines of Peru, most of the silver mines of Europe were abandoned. The value of silver was so much reduced that their produce could no longer pay the expense of working them or replace, with a profit, the food, clothes, lodging, and other necessaries consumed in that operation. This was also the case with the mines of Cuba and St. Domingo, and even with the ancient mines of Peru after the discovery of those of Potosi. Since the price of every metal at every mine is thus regulated in some measure by its price at the most fertile mine in the world that is actually worked, at most mines it can do little more than pay the expense of working and can seldom afford a very high rent to the landlord. This suggests that rent at most mines makes up but a small share of the price of the coarse metals and a still smaller share of that of the precious metals. Ultimately, labour and profit make up the greater part of both.

Since the price of every metal at every mine is thus regulated in some measure by its price at the most fertile mine in the world that is actually worked, at most mines it can do little more than pay the expense of working, and can seldom afford a very high rent to the landlord. This suggests that rent at most mines makes up but a small share of the price of the coarse metals, and a still smaller share of that of the precious metals. Labour and profit make up the greater part of both.

title: Dracula
input: The group proceeded to the back of the house, where they encountered a kitchen window. The Professor retrieved a small surgical saw from his case and handed it to a companion, indicating the iron bars protecting the window. The bars were cut through quickly, and using a long, thin knife, they managed to push back the sash fastening and open the window. The Professor entered first, followed by his companion. They observed that the kitchen and nearby servants' quarters were unoccupied. As they explored further, they discovered four servant-women lying on the dining-room floor, illuminated only by faint light filtering through the shutters. Their heavy breathing and the strong smell of laudanum indicated they were in a compromised state. The Professor and his companion exchanged glances, and he noted that they would address the women later. They then ascended to Lucy’s room. Briefly pausing at the door to listen for any sounds, they heard nothing and with anxious expressions, they gently opened the door and entered the room.

There was no one in the kitchen or in the servants’ rooms, which were close at hand. title: Dracula
input:
After some time, I left him. The attendant informs me that he remained quiet until just before dawn, when he began to grow uneasy and eventually became violent. This continued until he fell into a paroxysm that exhausted him to the point of fainting into a sort of coma.

For three nights, the same pattern has occurred: violent throughout the day, then quiet from moonrise to sunrise. I wish I could find some clue as to the cause. It would almost seem as though some influence comes and goes. A fortunate idea has occurred to me. Tonight we shall pit sane minds against mad ones. He escaped before without our assistance; tonight he shall escape with it. We shall give him an opportunity, and have the men ready to follow in case they are needed.

title: Dracula
input: A sound stirred me awake, perhaps the distant, sorrowful howling of dogs coming from far below in the valley, which I could not see. The sound seemed to resonate in my ears, and the dust particles around me appeared to shift shapes in response to it as they moved in the moonlight. I felt a struggle within me, as if my instincts—or perhaps my very essence—were trying to respond to this call. It was as though I were becoming entranced. The dust danced more rapidly, and the moonlight appeared to tremble as it passed through the surrounding darkness. Gradually, these lights formed vague, ghostly figures. Suddenly, I felt fully alert and bolted from the area, crying out in fear. The shapes that emerged from the moonlight were those of three spectral women, a haunting presence that I was destined to encounter. I sought refuge in my room, where the brightness of the lamp provided a sense of comfort, free from the moon’s eerie glow.

Louder it seemed to ring in my ears, and the floating motes of dust to take new shapes to the sound as they danced in the moonlight. I felt myself struggling to awake to some call of my instincts; nay, my very soul was struggling, and my half-remembered sensibilities were striving to answer the call. I was becoming hypnotised! Quicker and quicker danced the dust; the moonbeams seemed to quiver as they went by me into the mass of gloom beyond. More and more they gathered till they seemed to take dim phantom shapes. And then I started, broad awake and in full possession of my senses, and ran screaming from the place. The phantom shapes, which were becoming gradually materialised from the moonbeams, were those of the three ghostly women to whom I was doomed. I fled, and felt somewhat safer in my own room, where there was no moonlight and where the lamp was burning brightly.

Slowly, the light made shapes, ghostly and unclear. Then I snapped awake, scared, and ran into my room. The lamp’s light felt safe, keeping me away from the moon’s cold shine.

title: Dracula
input: I took his hand and made him a promise. I held the door open as he walked away, watching him enter his room and close the door behind him. As I stood there without moving, I noticed one of the maids quietly pass by in the hallway—she had her back to me and did not see me—before entering the room where Lucy was. This moment touched me. Devotion can often be uncommon, and we tend to feel a deep sense of gratitude towards those who show it willingly to the ones we care about. Here was a young woman putting aside her understandable fears of death to keep vigil by the side of her beloved mistress, ensuring that the poor body would not be alone until it was finally laid to rest. This act reflects the depth of human connection and kindness.

Devotion is so rare, and we are so grateful to those who show it unasked to those we love. Here was a poor girl putting aside the terrors which she naturally had of death to go watch alone by the bier of the mistress whom she loved, so that the poor clay might not be lonely till laid to eternal rest....

input: On May 18, the individual revisited the room during daylight to seek clarity about the situation. title: On Liberty
input: The concentration of all significant talent within the governing body can ultimately hinder its mental activity and capacity for progress. As a collective entity, the officials operate within a system that relies heavily on established rules, which can lead to complacency and habitual routines. When they do deviate from this routine, it often results in unexamined ideas influenced by prominent individuals within the group. The only effective way to counterbalance these opposing tendencies—complacency and impulsive ideas—is through the scrutiny of equally capable individuals outside the governing body. This highlights the necessity for independent avenues to cultivate talent and provide the experiences needed for sound judgment in practical matters. To ensure a proficient and innovative group of officials, it is crucial that not all tasks that nurture the skills needed for governance are monopolized by the governing body. This approach helps prevent the decline of the bureaucracy into a mere adherence to outdated practices.
human: It is not, also, to be forgotten, that the absorption of all the principal ability of the country into the governing body is fatal, sooner or later, to the mental activity and progressiveness of the body itself. Banded together as they are - working a system which, like all systems, necessarily proceeds in a great measure by fixed rules - the official body are under the constant temptation of sinking into indolent routine, or, if they now and then desert that mill-horse round, of rushing into some half-examined crudity which has struck the fancy of some leading member of the corps: and the sole check to these closely allied, though seemingly opposite, tendencies, the only stimulus which can keep the ability of the body itself up to a high standard, is liability to the watchful criticism of equal ability outside the body. It is indispensable, therefore, that the means should exist, independently of the government, of forming such ability, and furnishing it with the opportunities and experience necessary for a correct judgment of great practical affairs. If we would possess permanently a skilful and efficient body of functionaries - above all, a body able to originate and willing to adopt improvements; if we would not have our bureaucracy degenerate into a pedantocracy, this body must not engross all the occupations which form and cultivate the faculties required for the government of mankind.
base: When all the key talent is inside the leadership, it can slow down their thinking and stop them from moving forward. As a group, the officials work in a system full of old rules, which can make them lazy and stick to the same things all the time. When they break away from that routine, their new ideas are often shaped by the big names in the group. The only way to stop this from happening is to have people outside the group who are just as good at checking their work. This shows that there needs to be other ways to develop talent and give people the experience to make smart decisions. To have a group of officials who are both good and creative, it’s important that not all the training and work that helps them learn how to run things are done only by the leaders. This helps stop the bureaucracy from just following old ways without thinking.
finetuned: The concentration of all this great talent in the governing body, at last, so stifles its mental activity and its capacity for progress, that it becomes a mere automaton, governed by the rules of its own system, which are too numerous and too unchangeable to allow it to move except by the most mechanical habit. When it does move, it moves with ideas not examined, but suggested by the great men in the body. The only antidote to the poison of the two opposing diseases, complacency and the suggestion of great men, is the examination by men of equal capacity, but not in the governing body. Hence the need for independent channels of development and experience in order to acquire the judgment necessary for the sound judgment of practical affairs. To have a group of officials both proficient and original, it is necessary that not all the tasks which develop the talents necessary for the government should be monopolized by the governing body itself. Otherwise the bureaucracy will eventually become a mere copyist of the old ways.

title: On Liberty
input: I have saved for the last a large class of questions about the limits of government interference. These questions are closely connected with the subject of this Essay, but strictly speaking they do not belong to it. In these cases, the reasons against interference do not rest on the principle of liberty. The question is not about restraining the actions of individuals but about helping them. It is asked whether the government should do something for their benefit, or cause it to be done, instead of leaving it to be done by the individuals themselves, either singly or in voluntary combination.

title: On Liberty
input:
There exists a realm of action where society, as a collective, tends to have only an indirect interest, which includes aspects of a person's life and behavior that primarily impact themselves. While it is possible that these aspects may also affect others, this occurs only with their free and informed consent and participation. When referring to affecting oneself, it is important to note that this is in a direct and initial sense; what influences an individual may subsequently influence others through that individual. This potential for broader impact will be addressed later. Thus, this area represents the appropriate domain of personal liberty. 

It encompasses, first, the inner realm of consciousness, which calls for freedom of conscience in a broad sense. This includes the freedom to think and feel, as well as complete freedom of opinion and sentiment on all matters, whether practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The freedom to express and share opinions might appear to be governed by a different principle, since it pertains to an individual’s actions that involve others. However, it is often almost as significant as the freedom of thought itself and is largely based on similar reasoning, making it practically inseparable from it. Second, this principle advocates for the liberty of personal tastes and pursuits, allowing individuals to design their lives according to their own characters and to act as they wish, provided that their actions do not harm others, regardless of whether those others may perceive their choices as unwise or misguided. Third, from this individual liberty arises the freedom to form associations among individuals, enabling them to unite for any purpose that does not cause harm to others, assuming that those involved are of legal age and are not coerced or misled. In summary, the domain of human liberty encompasses individual thought, expression, personal pursuits, and the freedom to associate, all under the condition that these do not harm others.
human: But there is a sphere of action in which society, as distinguished from the individual, has, if any, only an indirect interest; comprehending all that portion of a person's life and conduct which affects only himself, or if it also affects others, only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent and participation. When I say only himself, I mean directly, and in the first instance: for whatever affects himself, may affect others through himself; and the objection which may be grounded on this contingency, will receive consideration in the sequel. This, then, is the appropriate region of human liberty. It comprises, first, the inward domain of consciousness; demanding liberty of conscience, in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions may seem to fall under a different principle, since it belongs to that part of the conduct of an individual which concerns other people; but, being almost of as much importance as the liberty of thought itself, and resting in great part on the same reasons, is practically inseparable from it. Secondly, the principle requires liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow: without impediment from our fellow-creatures, so long as what we do does not harm them, even though they should think our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong. Thirdly, from this liberty of each individual, follows the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived.
base:
There is a space where society as a whole isn’t directly involved, and it includes parts of a person’s life that mainly affect themselves. These parts might also affect others, but only if those others agree and are aware. When it comes to things that affect a person directly, it’s the start of a chain. What influences one person can later influence others through that person. That bigger effect will come up later. So this is where personal freedom belongs.

It starts with the inner world of a person’s mind, which needs freedom of thought and feeling. That includes the right to think and feel whatever they want, and to have any opinions on any subject—practical, scientific, moral, or religious. The right to talk about those opinions might seem different because it involves others. But it’s just as important as the right to think, and it’s based on the same reasons. So it’s almost like one without the other. Next, there’s the right to choose what you like and do what you want, as long as it doesn’t hurt others. Others might not see your choices as good, but that doesn’t matter. Finally, people can join together for any purpose as long as it doesn’t hurt others, and as long as they’re old enough and not forced or tricked. In short, freedom includes thinking, speaking, choosing what to do, and joining with others, as long as it doesn’t hurt anyone.

There is a sphere of action where society, as a whole, has only an indirect interest, which is in the life and conduct of an individual, which is primarily his own, though possibly also others'. But this only happens with their free and willing consent and co-operation. When I speak of affecting oneself, I mean this in a direct and primary sense: what affects an individual may affect others by means of him. This wider effect will be considered in its proper place. This is therefore the sphere of individual liberty.

It includes, first, the inner sphere of consciousness, requiring freedom of conscience in the broad sense. This is the freedom to think and to feel, and the complete freedom of opinion and sentiment on all matters, whether practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The freedom of expression and communication may seem to be governed by a different principle, because it concerns an individual's action which affects others. But it is almost as important as the freedom of thought itself, and is largely based on similar reasoning, and is therefore in practice inseparable from it. Second, this principle advocates the liberty of personal tastes and pursuits, that individuals may shape their lives according to their own characters, and act as they please, so long as they do not injure others, whether those others may think their choice unwise or mistaken. Third, from this individual liberty arises the freedom of association among individuals, that they may associate together for any purpose which does not injure others, provided they are of legal age and not compelled or misled.

title: On Liberty
input: It is worth noting that there exist numerous acts which, while they may only cause direct harm to the individuals who engage in them, should not be subject to legal prohibition. However, when such acts are performed in public, they constitute a breach of social decorum and, consequently, may be legitimately restricted under the category of offenses against others. Offenses against decency exemplify this concept; further elaboration on these matters is unnecessary, particularly since they are only tangentially related to our primary topic. The objection to public display is equally applicable to many actions that are not inherently reprehensible or perceived as such.
human: Again, there are many acts which, being directly injurious only to the agents themselves, ought not to be legally interdicted, but which, if done publicly, are a violation of good manners and coming thus within the category of offences against others may rightfully be prohibited. Of this kind are offences against decency; on which it is unnecessary to dwell, the rather as they are only connected indirectly with our subject, the objection to publicity being equally strong in the case of many actions not in themselves condemnable, nor supposed to be so.
base: Many actions cause harm only to those who do them and shouldn’t be illegal. But when done in public, they break social rules and can be properly restricted as offenses against others. Examples like offenses against decency show this. There’s no need to go into more detail, since they’re only loosely connected to our main point. The same argument applies to many actions that aren’t really bad or seen that way.
finetuned: There are, however, many acts, which though they may only do direct harm to those who commit them, ought not to be made the subjects of a legal prohibition. But when committed in public, they are breaches of social decencies, and are therefore properly included among the offenses against others, and may be lawfully restrained under the head of them. Offences against decency are an instance of this; and more on this head is unnecessary, especially as they are only in a very slight degree connected with our present subject. The objection to the public exhibition is equally applicable to many acts which are not themselves vicious, or are not considered as such.

title: The Time Machine
input:
You must follow my reasoning with considerable care. It is worth noting that I shall have to challenge one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted. For instance, the geometry that they taught you at school is founded upon a misconception.

Furthermore, is it not rather a substantial matter to expect us to begin upon? said Filby, an argumentative person with red hair.

Moreover, I do not mean to ask you to accept anything without reasonable ground for it. Additionally, you will soon concede as much as I require from you. It is worth noting that you know of course that a mathematical line, a line of no thickness, has no real existence. They taught you that? In essence, neither has a mathematical plane. These things are mere abstractions.

You know of course that a mathematical line, a line of no thickness, has no real existence. They taught you that? Neither has a mathematical plane. These things are mere abstractions.”

title: The Time Machine
input: Doubts began to arise for me. I wondered why the Morlocks might have taken my Time Machine, as I felt fairly certain they were responsible. It also made me curious why, if the Eloi were in charge, they could not retrieve the machine for me. Additionally, I found myself questioning their overwhelming fear of the dark. I attempted to discuss these matters with Weena, but I was somewhat let down by her responses. Initially, she appeared not to understand my questions, and eventually, she seemed unwilling to engage with the topic. She shivered, indicating that it might be too distressing for her. When I pressed her for more information, perhaps a bit too insistently, she began to cry. Those were the only tears I witnessed during that Golden Age, apart from my own. Seeing her distress shifted my focus completely; I became more concerned with alleviating her sadness than with the Morlocks. Before long, she was smiling and clapping her hands while I carefully burned a match. Ultimately, this moment highlighted the complexities of our emotions in that time.

Why, too, if the Eloi were masters, could they not restore the machine to me? And why were they so terribly afraid of the dark? I proceeded, as I have said, to question Weena about this Underworld, but here again I was disappointed. At first she would not understand my questions, and presently she refused to answer them. She shivered as though the topic was unendurable. And when I pressed her, perhaps a little harshly, she burst into tears. They were the only tears, except my own, I ever saw in that Golden Age. When I saw them I ceased abruptly to trouble about the Morlocks, and was only concerned in banishing these signs of her human inheritance from Weena’s eyes. And very soon she was smiling and clapping her hands, while I solemnly burnt a match.

title: The War of the Worlds
input: I travel to London and observe the bustling crowds on Fleet Street and the Strand. It occurs to me that they are merely the phantoms of the past, haunting the thoroughfares that I have witnessed as silent and forlorn. These figures move back and forth, mere specters in a lifeless city, embodying a mockery of existence within a reanimated form. Furthermore, it is a peculiar experience to stand on Primrose Hill, as I did just one day prior to composing this final chapter. I behold the vast expanse of houses, appearing dim and blue through the haze of smoke and mist, gradually disappearing into the indistinct lower sky. I observe people strolling amidst the flower beds on the hill and sightseers gathered around the Martian machine that remains stationary. I hear the joyous noise of children at play and reflect on the time when I perceived all these sights as bright and distinct, sharp and silent, beneath the dawn of that last significant day.

And strange, too, it is to stand on Primrose Hill, as I did but a day before writing this last chapter, to see the great province of houses, dim and blue through the haze of the smoke and mist, vanishing at last into the vague lower sky, to see the people walking to and fro among the flower beds on the hill, to see the sight-seers about the Martian machine that stands there still, to hear the tumult of playing children, and to recall the time when I saw it all bright and clear-cut, hard and silent, under the dawn of that last great day....

I watch people walking in the flower beds and tourists around the Martian machine that doesn't move. I hear children laughing and think about when I saw all this as bright and clear, under the dawn of that last important day.

title: The War of the Worlds
input: At around six in the evening, I sat with my wife in the summerhouse, discussing the imminent battle with fervor. Suddenly, I heard a muffled explosion coming from the common, followed swiftly by a barrage of gunfire. Soon after, a violent crash reverberated nearby, shaking the ground beneath us. As I stepped onto the lawn, I witnessed the treetops near the Oriental College erupt in a smoky red flame, while the tower of the adjacent church collapsed into ruins. The pinnacle of the mosque had completely disappeared, and the roofline of the college appeared as though it had been struck by a heavy artillery shell. One of our chimneys cracked with a sound resembling a gunshot, then broke apart, sending debris tumbling onto the tiles and creating a pile of shattered red fragments on the flower bed beside my study window.
human: About six in the evening, as I sat at tea with my wife in the summerhouse talking vigorously about the battle that was lowering upon us, I heard a muffled detonation from the common, and immediately after a gust of firing. Close on the heels of that came a violent rattling crash, quite close to us, that shook the ground; and, starting out upon the lawn, I saw the tops of the trees about the Oriental College burst into smoky red flame, and the tower of the little church beside it slide down into ruin. The pinnacle of the mosque had vanished, and the roof line of the college itself looked as if a hundred-ton gun had been at work upon it. One of our chimneys cracked as if a shot had hit it, flew, and a piece of it came clattering down the tiles and made a heap of broken red fragments upon the flower bed by my study window.

Soon after, a loud crash shook the ground. I stepped onto the lawn and saw the trees near the Oriental College burning red with smoke. The church tower collapsed. The mosque's top was gone. The college's roof looked like it had been hit by a shell. One of our chimneys cracked like a gun shot, then broke, sending pieces onto the tiles and making a pile of red shards by my study window.

As I stepped on to the lawn, I saw the treetops near the Oriental College blazing in a smoky red flame; and the tower of the neighbouring church was in ruins; the pinnacle of the mosque had vanished altogether; the roof-line of the college looked as if it had been pierced through by a shell. One of our chimneys cracked with a sound like a shot, and then broke in two, falling upon the tiles, and making a heap of shattered red fragments on the flower-bed beside my study-window.

title: The War of the Worlds
input:
The artilleryman shared his observations about the types of individuals who still remained in London. 

"Not long ago," he mentioned, "some individuals managed to restore the electric lights, resulting in Regent Street and the Circus being brightly lit and filled with intoxicated individuals, both men and women, who appeared to be celebrating and making noise until dawn. This was recounted to me by someone who witnessed it. As daylight approached, they noticed a fighting-machine nearby the Langham, observing them. It’s unclear how long it had been there, but it likely startled some of the people present. The machine then moved down the street and collected nearly a hundred individuals who were either too inebriated or frightened to escape." 

In summary, the artilleryman painted a picture of a chaotic scene marked by both celebration and fear in the city.
human:
The artilleryman began to tell me of the sort of people who still remained in London.

“One night last week,” he said, “some fools got the electric light in order, and there was all Regent Street and the Circus ablaze, crowded with painted and ragged drunkards, men and women, dancing and shouting till dawn. A man who was there told me. And as the day came they became aware of a fighting-machine standing near by the Langham and looking down at them. Heaven knows how long he had been there. It must have given some of them a nasty turn. He came down the road towards them, and picked up nearly a hundred too drunk or frightened to run away.”

As day came, they saw a fighting-machine near the Langham watching them. It’s not clear how long it had been there, but it probably scared some people. The machine then moved down the street and picked up nearly a hundred people who were too drunk or too scared to run." 

In short, the artilleryman described a city full of chaos, with both celebration and fear.

title: The War of the Worlds
input:
She was moving swiftly, appearing within moments to be positioned midway between the steamboat and the Martians, a dark silhouette against the vast, flat stretch of the Essex coast. 

Suddenly, the leading Martian lowered his tube and released a canister of black gas toward the ironclad. The canister struck her left side and deflected off, creating a dark plume that rolled out to sea, a flowing mass of black smoke from which the ironclad swiftly escaped. To the observers on the steamboat, sitting low in the water with the sun glaring in their eyes, it appeared as if she was already in the midst of the Martians.

It hit her larboard side and glanced off in an inky jet that rolled away to seaward, an unfolding torrent of Black Smoke, from which the ironclad drove clear. To the watchers from the steamer, low in the water and with the sun in their eyes, it seemed as though she were already among the Martians.

title: The War of the Worlds
input: Unable to discern the situation from his window, my brother decided to step outside into the street just as the sky began to brighten with dawn's early light. The number of people rushing by, both on foot and in vehicles, seemed to increase with each passing moment. He heard shouts of “Black Smoke!” echoing through the crowd, and the repetition of such a widespread fear was likely to be contagious. As my brother stood uncertainly on the doorstep, he noticed another newsvendor approaching and quickly purchased a paper. The vendor was hurrying away with the others, selling his papers for a shilling each as he ran, reflecting a strange mixture of urgency and commerce. In summary, the scene captured the chaotic atmosphere of the moment, blending fear and the instinct to profit.
human: Unable from his window to learn what was happening, my brother went down and out into the street, just as the sky between the parapets of the houses grew pink with the early dawn. The flying people on foot and in vehicles grew more numerous every moment. “Black Smoke!” he heard people crying, and again “Black Smoke!” The contagion of such a unanimous fear was inevitable. As my brother hesitated on the door-step, he saw another newsvendor approaching, and got a paper forthwith. The man was running away with the rest, and selling his papers for a shilling each as he ran - a grotesque mingling of profit and panic.

More people were moving around the street, walking and in cars, getting busier every minute. He heard someone yell “Black Smoke!” and the way people kept saying it made him feel uneasy. Standing on the doorstep, he saw another newsboy coming and bought a paper. The vendor was running off, selling each paper for a shilling, moving fast like everyone else. It was a mix of fear and trying to make money.

Standing irresolute on the doorstep, he saw another newsboy coming up and bought a paper. The newsboy was running away with the others, selling his papers for a shilling apiece as he ran.

title: The War of the Worlds
input:
By eight o’clock, a number of boys and unemployed men had already commenced their journey to the common in order to observe the “dead men from Mars.” This was the form that the story took. I first became aware of it from my newspaper boy at approximately a quarter to nine when I ventured out to retrieve my Daily Chronicle. I was understandably startled and did not delay in making my way across the Ottershaw bridge to the sand-pits.

Upon my arrival, I discovered a small crowd of approximately twenty individuals gathered around the substantial hole in which the cylinder rested. I have previously described the appearance of that colossal object, embedded in the earth. The turf and gravel surrounding it appeared charred, as if subjected to a sudden explosion. It is likely that its impact had generated a flash of fire. Henderson and Ogilvy were not present. I believe they realized that there was nothing that could be accomplished at that moment and had departed to have breakfast at Henderson’s residence.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
input: Atalanta is not the first or the last maiden whom greed for gold has led to defile the temple of Love. Moreover, it is not only maidens but also men who, in the race of life, sink from the high and generous ideals of youth to the gambler's code of the stock exchange. In all our nation's striving, is the Gospel of Work not corrupted by the Gospel of Pay? This is so common that one half of people consider it normal. It is so unquestioned that we almost fear to ask whether the end of racing is gold and whether the proper aim of man is to be rich. If this is the fault of America, how dire a danger lies before a new land and a new city, lest Atlanta, stooping for mere gold, shall find that gold accursed.

So common is this that one-half think it normal; so unquestioned, that we almost fear to question if the end of racing is not gold, if the aim of man is not rightly to be rich. And if this is the fault of America, how dire a danger lies before a new land and a new city, lest Atlanta, stooping for mere gold, shall find that gold accursed!

title: The Souls of Black Folk
input: I have so far attempted to clarify the physical, economic, and political relations between Negroes and whites in the South as I have understood them, including crime and education for the reasons already given. Yet beyond these more tangible matters of human contact, there remains an essential part of any proper description of the South that is difficult to describe or define in terms easily understood by outsiders. It is, in short, the atmosphere of the land, the thought and feeling, and the countless small actions that together constitute daily life. In any community or nation, these small things are the most elusive to grasp and yet the most essential to a clear understanding of group life as a whole. What is true of all communities is especially true of the South, where, beyond written history and printed law, there has been unfolding for a generation a profound storm and stress of human souls, an intense ferment of feeling, and an intricate writhing of spirit such as few peoples have experienced. Within and beyond the somber veil of color, vast social forces have been at work: efforts for human betterment, movements toward disintegration and despair, tragedies and comedies in social and economic life, and a shifting and rising and falling of human hearts that have made this land one of mingled sorrow and joy, of change and excitement and unrest.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
input: The discovery of the golden fleece signifies a notable development; it has not only been located but is also being produced in its region of origin. The operation of cotton mills represents a significant aspect of the modern economy in the New South. Throughout the Carolinas and Georgia, extending into Mexico, one can observe the presence of these large, utilitarian structures, which, despite their simple appearance, are characterized by a bustling and noisy activity that contrasts with the surrounding landscape. This suggests that the Cotton Kingdom continues to play an important role, as its influence persists. Furthermore, markets that once resisted newcomers have gradually expanded overseas and have begun to move toward the Black Belt region, indicating a shift in economic dynamics.
human: And now the golden fleece is found; not only found, but, in its birthplace, woven. For the hum of the cotton-mills is the newest and most significant thing in the New South to-day. All through the Carolinas and Georgia, away down to Mexico, rise these gaunt red buildings, bare and homely, and yet so busy and noisy withal that they scarce seem to belong to the slow and sleepy land. Perhaps they sprang from dragons’ teeth. So the Cotton Kingdom still lives; the world still bows beneath her sceptre. Even the markets that once defied the parvenu have crept one by one across the seas, and then slowly and reluctantly, but surely, have started toward the Black Belt.

In the Carolinas and Georgia, all the way to Mexico, there are these big, plain buildings. Even though they look simple, they’re full of noise and activity, which is different from the land around them. This shows the Cotton Kingdom is still important, its influence still there. Also, markets that used to keep others out are now growing outside the country and are moving toward the Black Belt, showing the economy is changing.

The Cotton Kingdom is still in operation; its influence is still felt. Markets which once resisted the intrusion of foreigners have gradually expanded overseas and are now moving toward the Black Belt.

title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
input:
Moreover, he expressed, "My head is spinning. He has possessed himself of the situation for all these days; he had no reason to favor me; he must have been furious to witness his own displacement; yet, he has not destroyed this document." 

Furthermore, he seized the next paper; it was a concise note penned by the doctor, bearing a date at the top. "Oh, Poole!" the lawyer exclaimed, "he was alive and present on this day. It is implausible that he could have been disposed of in such a brief period; he must still be alive, he must have escaped! However, why would he have fled, and how? In that case, can we confidently label this as a suicide? Oh, we must exercise caution. I foresee that we may inadvertently entangle your master in a severe catastrophe."

title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
input: The besiegers, perhaps unsettled by the chaos they had just caused and the sudden silence that followed, instinctively stepped back and looked inside. Before them, in the gentle light of the lamp, was a cabinet, with a warm fire flickering and crackling in the hearth, the kettle softly whistling a delicate tune. A few drawers were ajar, and papers were neatly arranged on the business table, while closer to the fire, items were prepared for tea. It was likely the quietest room one might imagine, and, aside from the glass-fronted cabinets filled with chemicals, it could be described as one of the most ordinary spaces that night in London. Overall, it presented a striking contrast to the turmoil outside.

title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
input: Men have historically engaged others to carry out their illicit activities while maintaining their own safety and reputation. This highlights a unique phenomenon in which I was the first to employ this practice for personal enjoyment. I was able to navigate public life with an air of respectability, and, in an instant, shed that façade to embrace a sense of freedom. Ultimately, I found complete security in my concealed existence. This suggests a profound detachment; I did not even have to take direct responsibility for my actions. By simply retreating to my laboratory, allowing myself a brief moment to prepare and consume a concoction that I always kept at hand, I could make Edward Hyde disappear as easily as a breath vanishes from a mirror. In his place, I would quietly return home, tending to my studies with a sense of assurance that allowed me to dismiss any doubts about my character.
human: Men have before hired bravos to transact their crimes, while their own person and reputation sat under shelter. I was the first that ever did so for his pleasures. I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability, and in a moment, like a schoolboy, strip off these lendings and spring headlong into the sea of liberty. But for me, in my impenetrable mantle, the safety was complete. Think of it - I did not even exist! Let me but escape into my laboratory door, give me but a second or two to mix and swallow the draught that I had always standing ready; and whatever he had done, Edward Hyde would pass away like the stain of breath upon a mirror; and there in his stead, quietly at home, trimming the midnight lamp in his study, a man who could afford to laugh at suspicion, would be Henry Jekyll.

I moved through public life with dignity, and in a moment, I could drop that image and feel free. In the end, I found total safety in my hidden life. This shows a deep separation; I didn’t even have to be directly responsible. By going to my lab, taking a moment to prepare and drink the potion I always had, I could make Edward Hyde vanish like mist. Then I would go home quietly, taking care of my studies with the confidence that let me ignore any questions about who I was.

I was able to pass through the streets of London, and to be the talk of the world, and, in a moment, to cast off all this and to be as free as the birds in the air. I found perfect security in my hiding-place. I was not even obliged to be responsible for myself. I could go into my laboratory, take a little time to make myself ready and to drink a draught of that potion which I always kept in my hand, and then, in the twinkling of an eye, make Edward Hyde vanish away like a breath from a mirror, and, in his stead, quietly return home, and go on with my studies with a sense of confidence which enabled me to ignore any suspicion of my character.

title: Anne of Green Gables
input: October was a beautiful month at Green Gables. The birches in the hollow turned as golden as sunshine, the maples behind the orchard were royal crimson, and the wild cherry trees along the lane took on the loveliest shades of dark red and bronzy green, while the fields rested in their aftermath. One Saturday morning, Anne came dancing in with her arms full of gorgeous boughs. “Oh, Marilla,” she exclaimed, “I’m so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers. It would be terrible if we just skipped from September to November, wouldn’t it? Look at these maple branches. Don’t they give you a thrill—several thrills? I’m going to decorate my room with them.” This highlights how deeply Anne responds to the changing seasons, and her delight suggests a lively appreciation for the beauty around her. Ultimately, the passage conveys a simple, wholehearted joy in the month of October.

Anne couldn’t help but feel a strong dislike for the white-lace girl. In summary, the entire experience was proving to be more than a little overwhelming for her.

title: Anne of Green Gables
input: I suppose I must finish my lessons first. I will not allow myself to open that new book Jane lent me until I am through. However, it is a terrible temptation, Matthew. Even when I turn my back on it, I can see it there just as plain. Jane said she cried herself sick over it. I love a book that makes me cry. Nevertheless, I think I will carry that book into the sitting room and lock it in the jam closet and give you the key. You must not give it to me, Matthew, until my lessons are done, not even if I implore you on my bended knees. It is all very well to say resist temptation, but it is ever so much easier to resist it if you cannot get the key. And then shall I run down the cellar and get some russets, Matthew? Would you not like some russets?

title: Anne of Green Gables
input: Anne expressed her determination to engage with young girls respectfully, emphasizing that she would not laugh at their use of complex vocabulary, as she recognized the emotional impact this could have. She then recounted an experience with Diana, where they attempted to make taffy for the first time. Unfortunately, the taffy did not turn out well because neither of them had prior experience. During the process, Diana left Anne to stir while she prepared the plates, leading to the taffy burning. Additionally, a cat walked across one plate, resulting in its disposal. Despite these setbacks, Anne found the activity to be enjoyable. Upon returning home, Mrs. Barry invited Anne to visit frequently, while Diana affectionately waved goodbye from the window. This highlights Anne's sense of joy and connection, as she noted feeling inspired to create a new prayer to commemorate the day's events.
human: “Well, anyway, when I am grown up,” said Anne decidedly, “I’m always going to talk to little girls as if they were too, and I’ll never laugh when they use big words. I know from sorrowful experience how that hurts one’s feelings. After tea Diana and I made taffy. The taffy wasn’t very good, I suppose because neither Diana nor I had ever made any before. Diana left me to stir it while she buttered the plates and I forgot and let it burn; and then when we set it out on the platform to cool the cat walked over one plate and that had to be thrown away. But the making of it was splendid fun. Then when I came home Mrs. Barry asked me to come over as often as I could and Diana stood at the window and threw kisses to me all the way down to Lover’s Lane. I assure you, Marilla, that I feel like praying tonight and I’m going to think out a special brand-new prayer in honor of the occasion.”

title: Anne of Green Gables
input:
After Anne left, Marilla attended to her evening chores, feeling quite unsettled. She was deeply concerned about her valuable brooch. What if Anne had misplaced it? It was infuriating that the girl denied taking it when it was clear to anyone that she must have. Her innocent face only added to Marilla’s frustration.

“I cannot think of anything worse,” Marilla reflected as she nervously shelled peas. “I do not believe she intended to steal it. She probably took it to play with or to fuel her imagination. It is obvious she must have taken it, as no one else had been in that room since she left, according to her own account, until I went up tonight. The brooch is undoubtedly missing. I assume she has lost it and is too frightened to admit it for fear of punishment. It is upsetting to consider that she tells lies. This is a far more serious issue than her earlier temper. It is a heavy burden to care for a child whom one cannot trust. Deception and dishonesty are what she has shown. I must admit I feel worse about that than about the brooch itself. If she had only told the truth, I would not feel as troubled.”

She’s just taken it to play with or help along that imagination of hers. title: Anne of Green Gables
input:
Despite her intense dislike for Gilbert, she loved Diana deeply, with the full force of her passionate heart, equally strong in its preferences and aversions. One evening, Marilla returned from the orchard carrying a basket of apples and discovered Anne sitting by the east window in the fading light, crying uncontrollably.

"It is about Diana," Anne sobbed dramatically. "I love Diana so much, Marilla. I cannot imagine living without her. However, I know that as we grow older, Diana will marry and leave me. What will I do then? I detest her husband; I truly despise him. I have envisioned the entire event—the wedding and everything. Diana will be dressed in white, adorned with a veil, looking as beautiful and regal as a queen, while I will stand as the bridesmaid in a lovely dress with puffed sleeves, concealing a broken heart beneath my smiling exterior. Then I will have to say goodbye to Diana…" At this point, Anne completely broke down and wept with escalating sorrow.

title: Little Women
input:
Margaret, despite her minor vanities, possessed a kind and devout character that subtly impacted her sisters, particularly Jo, who had a deep affection for her and followed her guidance due to the gentle manner in which it was offered. This highlights the bond they shared.

In a serious tone, Meg addressed her sisters, looking from the disheveled one beside her to the two in the adjoining room wearing nightcaps. She stated that their mother wanted them to engage with certain books meaningfully, emphasizing the importance of starting immediately. Meg noted that they had previously been diligent about this practice, but since their father’s departure and the ongoing turmoil of war, they had fallen behind. She acknowledged that while her sisters could choose their own paths, she intended to keep her book on the table and read a little each morning upon waking, believing it would benefit her and help her navigate the day. Ultimately, this reflects Meg's commitment to maintaining a sense of routine and devotion in challenging times.

title: The Age of Innocence
input:

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
input:
Folklore, legends, myths, and fairy tales have accompanied childhood throughout history, as every vibrant child possesses a natural and profound appreciation for extraordinary, enchanting, and evidently unreal narratives. The winged fairies depicted by the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen have undoubtedly delivered more joy to youthful hearts than any other human creation.

Moreover, the traditional fairy tale, having fulfilled its purpose for countless generations, may now be regarded as “historical” within the children’s literary canon. The time has arrived for a new collection of “wonder tales,” in which the conventional genie, dwarf, and fairy are omitted, along with all the grotesque and terrifying incidents crafted by their authors to convey a harrowing moral lesson. Contemporary education encompasses moral instruction; consequently, the modern child seeks solely entertainment in these wonder tales and willingly discards any unpleasant occurrences.

Yet the old time fairy tale, having served for generations, may now be classed as “historical” in the children’s library; for the time has come for a series of newer “wonder tales” in which the stereotyped genie, dwarf and fairy are eliminated, together with all the horrible and blood-curdling incidents devised by their authors to point a fearsome moral to each tale. Modern education includes morality; therefore the modern child seeks only entertainment in its wonder tales and gladly dispenses with all disagreeable incident.

title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: It is worth noting that the reason it is natural to refer to this principle as a law of thought lies in the fact that we rely on thought, rather than external observation, to convince ourselves of its necessary truth. After we have observed that a tree is a beech, we do not need to examine it again to confirm that it is not also a beech; our reasoning alone informs us that such a contradiction is impossible. However, the conclusion that the law of contradiction is solely a law of thought is, in fact, erroneous. When we accept the law of contradiction, we do not assert that the mind is constructed in such a way that it must adhere to this law. Rather, this acceptance emerges as a subsequent outcome of psychological reflection, which itself presupposes an initial belief in the law of contradiction. The belief in this law pertains to the nature of reality and not merely to the realm of thought. It is not, for example, the conviction that if we consider a specific tree to be a beech, we cannot simultaneously consider it to be not a beech; instead, it is the assertion that if the tree is a beech, it cannot concurrently be not a beech. Consequently, the law of contradiction pertains to the nature of things rather than merely to thoughts; while the belief in the law of contradiction qualifies as a thought, the law itself constitutes a fact regarding the entities in the world. If the assertion we make when we accept the law of contradiction were not true concerning the nature of reality, the necessity of our belief would not render the law of contradiction true; this indicates that the law cannot be classified solely as a law of thought.
human: Now what makes it natural to call this principle a law of thought is that it is by thought rather than by outward observation that we persuade ourselves of its necessary truth. When we have seen that a tree is a beech, we do not need to look again in order to ascertain whether it is also not a beech; thought alone makes us know that this is impossible. But the conclusion that the law of contradiction is a law of thought is nevertheless erroneous. What we believe, when we believe the law of contradiction, is not that the mind is so made that it must believe the law of contradiction. This belief is a subsequent result of psychological reflection, which presupposes the belief in the law of contradiction. The belief in the law of contradiction is a belief about things, not only about thoughts. It is not, e.g., the belief that if we think a certain tree is a beech, we cannot at the same time think that it is not a beech; it is the belief that if the tree is a beech, it cannot at the same time be not a beech. Thus the law of contradiction is about things, and not merely about thoughts; and although belief in the law of contradiction is a thought, the law of contradiction itself is not a thought, but a fact concerning the things in the world. If this, which we believe when we believe the law of contradiction, were not true of the things in the world, the fact that we were compelled to think it true would not save the law of contradiction from being false; and this shows that the law is not a law of thought.

title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: In derivative knowledge, it is essential that our ultimate premises possess a certain degree of self-evidence, as must the connection between these premises and the conclusions derived from them. For instance, consider a reasoning process in geometry. It is insufficient for the axioms upon which we base our reasoning to be self-evident; it is equally necessary that, at each stage of the reasoning, the relationship between premises and conclusions be self-evident as well. In complex reasoning, this connection often exhibits only a minimal degree of self-evidence; consequently, errors in reasoning are not unlikely when the difficulty of the task is considerable.
human: In derivative knowledge our ultimate premisses must have some degree of self-evidence, and so must their connexion with the conclusions deduced from them. Take for example a piece of reasoning in geometry. It is not enough that the axioms from which we start should be self-evident: it is necessary also that, at each step in the reasoning, the connexion of premiss and conclusion should be self-evident. In difficult reasoning, this connexion has often only a very small degree of self-evidence; hence errors of reasoning are not improbable where the difficulty is great.
base: In derivative knowledge, our starting points need to be pretty clear on their own. The links between those starting points and the ideas we build from them also need to be clear. Think about geometry. Just having the basic rules be obvious isn’t enough. At every step, the way the rules connect to the results has to be obvious too. In tricky problems, those links are often not so clear. So when things get complicated, mistakes are more likely.

title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: As the number of observed cases in which a thing of type A is found associated with a thing of type B increases, and provided that no cases of failed association are known, it becomes more probable that A is always associated with B. Under the same circumstances, a sufficient number of cases of the association of A with B will make it nearly certain that A is always associated with B, and will cause this general law to approach certainty without limit.

title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: If the previous account holds some validity, it appears that our understanding of truths may largely depend on our intuitive knowledge. As such, it seems worthwhile to explore the nature and extent of intuitive knowledge, similar to how we previously examined knowledge by acquaintance. However, knowledge of truths introduces an additional challenge that does not typically arise with knowledge of objects: the issue of error. It can often happen that some of our beliefs are mistaken, which leads us to consider how we might distinguish knowledge from error, if it is possible at all. This concern is not present in the context of knowledge by acquaintance, since, regardless of the specific object of acquaintance, even in cases like dreams and hallucinations, no error occurs as long as we focus on the immediate object. Error tends to arise only when we interpret the immediate object, or sense-datum, as indicative of some external physical object. Therefore, the challenges associated with knowledge of truths may be more complex than those linked to knowledge of objects. To begin addressing the issues related to knowledge of truths, let us first investigate the nature and scope of our intuitive judgments.

Around this time, a motivated young reporter from New York visited Gatsby’s residence and inquired if he had any statements to make. 

After a brief and somewhat unclear exchange, it became apparent that the reporter had heard Gatsby's name mentioned in his office, though he either chose not to disclose the context or did not fully grasp it. This was his day off, and he had taken the initiative to investigate further. 

While his approach was somewhat random, it suggested that the reporter's instincts were accurate. Gatsby's growing notoriety, fueled by the many guests who had enjoyed his hospitality and shared their experiences, had reached a level where he was nearly considered newsworthy. Various contemporary legends, such as the rumored "underground pipeline to Canada," became associated with him, and one persistent tale claimed he did not actually reside in a house, but rather in a boat designed to resemble a house, which was allegedly moved secretly along the Long Island coast. Ultimately, it remains unclear why these fabrications appealed to James Gatz from North Dakota.

title: The Great Gatsby
input: The appeal of New York lies in its vibrant nighttime atmosphere, characterized by a dynamic interplay of people and vehicles that captivates the observer. Walking along Fifth Avenue, one might find themselves drawn to the romantic figures in the crowd, imagining brief connections that go unnoticed by others. This act of imagination can extend to envisioning these individuals in their private lives, suggesting a fleeting intimacy that is both thrilling and elusive. However, amidst this enchanting urban twilight, there is also a sense of poignant loneliness that can be felt not only by oneself but also by others. The image of young clerks lingering in front of shop windows, waiting for their solitary meals, reflects the bittersweet nature of those moments, highlighting the contrast between the vibrancy of the city and the isolation experienced by some of its inhabitants.
human: I began to like New York, the racy, adventurous feel of it at night, and the satisfaction that the constant flicker of men and women and machines gives to the restless eye. I liked to walk up Fifth Avenue and pick out romantic women from the crowd and imagine that in a few minutes I was going to enter into their lives, and no one would ever know or disapprove. Sometimes, in my mind, I followed them to their apartments on the corners of hidden streets, and they turned and smiled back at me before they faded through a door into warm darkness. At the enchanted metropolitan twilight I felt a haunting loneliness sometimes, and felt it in others - poor young clerks who loitered in front of windows waiting until it was time for a solitary restaurant dinner - young clerks in the dusk, wasting the most poignant moments of night and life.
base: New York’s appeal is in its night life, where people and cars move together, making the city feel alive. On Fifth Avenue, you might notice couples in the crowd, and you wonder about their stories, the moments they share that others don’t see. You might imagine their lives, the quiet things they do alone. But in the middle of all that energy, there’s also a quiet sadness. You see young workers standing by store windows, waiting for their own meals, and it makes you think about how even in a busy city, some people feel alone. It’s a mix of excitement and loneliness, a feeling that’s everywhere but never quite spoken.
finetuned: It is the night-life of New York that is so delicious to me. The mass of people and automobiles that rush to and fro on Fifth Avenue, the beautiful women who stroll in and out of the crowd, the lovers who pass in secret glances, the clever young men who smile at a girl’s eyes and are never noticed, the girls who dream of an hour’s intimacy with some strange man, the strange men who dream of a girl’s eyes, the shop windows where young clerks stand, waiting for their own solitary meals, the city in its dreamy twilight - it is all so delicious. It is all so delicious. It is all so lonely. It is all so lonely.

input: The following April, Daisy welcomed the birth of her daughter, after which they relocated to France for a year. I encountered them one spring in Cannes, subsequently in Deauville, before they returned to Chicago to establish their permanent residence. As you are aware, Daisy enjoyed considerable popularity in Chicago. They mingled with a vibrant social circle, composed largely of affluent and youthful individuals who exhibited a penchant for exuberance; however, Daisy emerged with an impeccably pristine reputation. This may be attributed, at least in part, to her choice to abstain from alcohol. It is a significant advantage to refrain from drinking within a milieu characterized by heavy consumption, as it enables one to exercise discretion and, moreover, to time any personal indiscretions in such a way that they remain unnoticed or unaddressed by others. It is conceivable that Daisy never engaged in romantic affairs at all; nevertheless, there exists an undeniable allure in the quality of her voice.

title: The Great Gatsby
input: There was dancing taking place on the canvas in the garden, where older men might often be seen guiding young girls in circles that lacked grace, while couples, perhaps seeking to appear fashionable, held each other in somewhat awkward positions along the edges. Many single girls danced alone or took turns with the orchestra, giving the banjo or drums a brief rest. By midnight, the atmosphere had likely become even more festive. A well-known tenor sang in Italian, while a somewhat infamous contralto performed in a jazz style. In between musical numbers, people could be observed performing acts around the garden, accompanied by bursts of cheerful laughter rising into the warm summer night. A pair of performers, who turned out to be the girls in yellow, presented a playful act in costume. Champagne was served in glasses that were larger than typical finger bowls. As the moon rose higher, a shimmering triangle of silver scales appeared in the Sound, gently responding to the rhythmic sound of banjos played on the lawn. Overall, the scene was one of lively celebration and enjoyment.

title: The Great Gatsby
input:
At eight o’clock, when the streets of the Forties were filled with numerous taxicabs heading to the theater district, I experienced a sense of melancholy. The taxis were packed with people, their voices mingled with laughter, and the glow of lighted cigarettes created indistinct patterns in the air. Imagining myself among the crowd, sharing in their joy, I wished them well.

For some time, I lost track of Jordan Baker, but I eventually encountered her again during the summer. Initially, I felt a sense of pride in being seen with her since she was a well-known golf champion. However, my feelings deepened into a kind of gentle intrigue. The aloof expression she presented to the world seemed to mask something deeper—this suggests that many superficial behaviors often hide more significant truths. One day, during a house party in Warwick, I discovered what was beneath her facade. She had left a borrowed car in the rain with the top down and then lied about it. This incident triggered my recollection of a story about her that I had forgotten since that evening at Daisy’s. At her first major golf tournament, an incident arose that nearly became a scandal; it was alleged that she had moved her ball from a poor position during the semifinal round. The controversy garnered significant attention, but it ultimately faded when a caddy retracted his statement and another witness admitted uncertainty. The incident and her name became linked in my memory.

The incident and the name had remained together in my mind.
